watches.title: Hormuz Watch
watches.dek: Tanker movement through the world's most important oil chokepoint: baseline, conflict disruption, and the current transit picture.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the barrel count behind the price: the Strait of Hormuz carries roughly one-fifth of the world's petroleum liquids, and every transit number here is a proxy for how much of that supply is actually moving. Each bullet carries its vintage, so read the wartime vessel counts against the pre-war baseline of about 20 to 21 million barrels per day, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) figure for the first half of 2025.
watches.wcs_stakes: Hormuz is the world's main sour export artery, and when it closes, the sour barrels Western Canadian Select (WCS) competes with disappear first, which is why Canadian differentials tightened as the war cut Gulf flows. Fewer Iranian, Iraqi, and Saudi sour barrels reaching Asia and Europe forces buyers onto substitute grades, bidding up Mars and other Atlantic Basin sours alongside WCS. If Hormuz transits normalize, the returning sour supply is the fastest way Canadian differentials soften again.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, Hormuz is the supply-side risk premium inside every WCS print. Vessel counts and the EIA's quarterly volume series tell you whether the chokepoint is loosening before the price does. The moment Gulf sour barrels flow freely again, expect the bid under Canadian heavies to fade with them.

bullets.text: EIA estimated oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 20.9 million b/d in the first half of 2025, roughly 15 million b/d of crude oil and condensate plus about 5.5 million b/d of refined petroleum products.
IEA estimated about 20 million b/d of crude and products moved through Hormuz in 2025, roughly 25% of global seaborne oil trade and about 20% of world petroleum liquids consumption.
Of the Hormuz total, nearly 15 million b/d was crude oil, about 34% of all global crude oil trade in 2025; roughly 80% of the oil was destined for Asian markets.
Destination split of Hormuz crude in 2025: China ~25%, India ~19%, Japan ~13%, South Korea ~11%, other Asia ~17%, Europe ~9%, US ~3%; China and India together took 44% of flows.
Saudi Arabia is the dominant single-country contributor to Hormuz crude flows, about 38% or roughly 5.5 million b/d; Iraq, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar and Iran make up the rest.
EIA estimated one-fifth of global LNG trade moved through Hormuz in 2024, primarily Qatari cargoes, IEA's February 2026 factsheet put it at almost 20% of global LNG exports.
bullets.source: EIA Today in Energy (via GitHub essay)

bullets.text: US crude and condensate imports through Hormuz were about 7% of total US crude and condensate imports in 2024 and about 2% of US petroleum liquids consumption.
bullets.source: EIA Today in Energy (via GitHub essay)

bullets.text: Saudi Arabia and the UAE have pipelines capable of bypassing the strait, but together they could provide only about 4.7 million b/d of bypass capacity, a fraction of normal ~21 million b/d traffic.
bullets.vintage: Data: EIA estimate current through 2026; accessed 2026-09-23

bullets.text: Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline carries crude from the kingdom's eastern producing region to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing Saudi oil to reach water without passing through Hormuz; it has become the main bypass artery during the current conflict.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on NBC's Meet the Press that Iran is fully prepared for the war to resume, even a doomsday war, while remaining ready for diplomacy; CNN reported the White House rejected the proposal because it doubts Tehran is negotiating in good faith.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on September 27 that Tehran's conditions for reopening the strait are unchanged and that he had received nothing from mediators Qatar and Pakistan since the United States rejected the plan, insisting only a negotiated solution can end the standoff.

President Trump told reporters on September 26 that he had rejected Iran's seven-day proposal to reopen the strait, saying Tehran wants a deal because it is losing badly under the US naval blockade and calling the blockade the greatest in military history.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented a seven-day proposal at the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, transmitted to Washington through Qatar: Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal maritime passage and resume nuclear talks within seven days if the United States ends the naval blockade, waives sanctions on Iranian oil, releases at least $12 billion in frozen assets, and holds a ceasefire on all fronts, including Lebanon and Yemen.
bullets.source: The Hindu BusinessLine (citing the Associated Press)

bullets.text: The Wall Street Journal reported on September 26 that President Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz proposal, telling aides he doubts Tehran will meet his demands and expects a renewed bombing campaign after the November midterms.

Two tankers were attacked on the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, four nautical miles off Khasab on the Musandam Peninsula: about four projectiles hit the two vessels at roughly 1910 UTC, one caught fire and the other's status was unknown, according to a report UKMTO received from a nearby vessel's master. Iran has not claimed responsibility.
The current war was triggered February 28, 2026 by joint US and Israeli strikes on Iran; Iran responded by closing commercial access to Hormuz through vessel attacks and sea mining.

As of September 20, 2026, US Central Command said its forces had redirected 109 commercial vessels to enforce compliance with the US maritime blockade on traffic to and from Iranian ports, a blockade resumed July 14, 2026.

On September 1, 2026, a commercial tanker was struck by at least three unknown projectiles while completing an outbound Hormuz transit about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman; no casualties were reported. A second reported tanker strike nearby (Saudi-flagged Sidr) was carried as reported but unconfirmed by that source.

Between September 16 and 18, 2026, three tankers were struck in the strait; the Togo-flagged product tanker Trend was hit September 16 near Khasab and caught fire before the crew extinguished it. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed the Trend attack, saying it was an illegal transit attempt, and warned any unauthorized passage would face 'destruction'.
A UKMTO security warning dated September 17, 2026 covered an attack 16 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman; the targeted vessel's crew were confirmed safe with no environmental impact.

UKMTO reported September 21, 2026 that an inbound tanker transiting the strait was struck by an unknown projectile; two crew members suffered minor injuries, the vessel continued under its own power, and no environmental impact was reported. An investigation is underway; the vessel's name and flag were not released.
UKMTO reported a second September 22 incident in which an LNG tanker was said to have been struck by an unknown projectile in the strait, with no injuries, the second attack reported that day.
bullets.source: London Channel News (via Qatar Tribune / DPA, citing UKMTO)

bullets.text: UKMTO issued an advisory after the September 21 strike urging vessels operating in the area to transit with caution and report suspicious activity to authorities.

sections.heading: Now vs normal: the transit picture

bullets.text: Kpler tracked nine Hormuz commodity-vessel transits on September 24, down from 14 the day before and below the 10-day average of about 18; Kpler estimated 33.7 million barrels of crude exported in the week beginning September 20, with 17 of the 19 crude tankers tracked that week being very large crude carriers, which is why barrel flows can run ahead of vessel counts.

Kpler data showed September crude transits through Hormuz rebounding to 10.1 million b/d month-to-date, up nearly 70.5 percent from the full month of August and the first time above 10 million b/d since the war began; Kpler's Matt Smith called it a solid rebound, while noting February moved just over 16 million b/d of crude in the war's first days.

EIA estimated LNG flows through Hormuz fell to 0.8 billion cubic feet per day in the second quarter of 2026, from about 10.5 to 11.4 billion cubic feet per day before the conflict; the agency said its figures supplement vessel tracking with origin, destination and route analysis because AIS signals have become unreliable in the conflict zone.

EIA's quarterly Hormuz series shows the collapse in stages: 20.4 million b/d in Q1 2025, 21.6 million b/d in Q4 2025 before the war, 14.6 million b/d in Q1 2026 after the February 28 strikes, then 4.9 million b/d in Q2 2026. The Q1 2026 split was about 10.7 million b/d of crude and condensate plus 3.9 million b/d of products, down from 14.3 and 6.1 a year earlier.
bullets.vintage: Data through Q2 2026; EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook reporting, Aug-Sep 2026

bullets.text: Trump told Axios on September 27 that Tehran had overplayed its hand and that the offer was what the United States might have accepted a year ago, adding he expects negotiations to resume this week and claiming more than 20 million barrels of oil transited the strait over the weekend, a figure a US defense official put at 22 million barrels; the figure is a US claim, not a tracker count.

Trump asserted on September 26 that the United States exercises complete control over the strait and said 29 ships transited the chokepoint over the past day, framing the blockade as the pressure forcing Tehran toward talks; the figure is a US claim, not a tracker count.

The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit by an unknown projectile on September 23, caught fire and went adrift, with UKMTO reporting one Indian seafarer killed and one injured; preliminary Kpler data cited by Reuters showed only two commodity vessels crossed the strait on September 21, against about 125 large commercial vessels per day before the war.
bullets.source: SAFETY4SEA (citing UKMTO; Kpler data via Reuters)

bullets.text: US Central Command said it had redirected 122 commercial vessels as of September 25, up from 115 on September 23 and 110 on September 21.

Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz held at 12 crossings on September 23, unchanged from September 22: about 10 vessels inbound and two outbound, per Windward data. Three inbound vessels used the southern US-assisted route and six took Iran's northern corridor; both outbound vessels used the southern route.

EIA figures show Hormuz oil flows fell from 21.6 million b/d in Q4 2025 to just 4.9 million b/d in Q2 2026, while Bab el-Mandeb flows rose from 5.4 to 8.1 million b/d, a major rerouting of the global oil transportation system.
Crossings through the strait fell to just four vessels on September 16, 2026, the same day as the first of that week's attacks.

Recent tracking shows commodity-carrying Hormuz transits averaging roughly 10 vessels per day versus a pre-war baseline of around 85–90; throughput has been reported as low as ~7% of normal in some periods.

IEA's September 2026 Oil Market Report said more than 10 million b/d of Gulf output remained shut in amid security risks; cumulative supply losses since February exceeded 507 million barrels of observed inventory draws.
bullets.vintage: Data through Aug 2026; report Sep 11, 2026; accessed 2026-09-23
bullets.source: Namibia Daily News (via Xinhua, citing IEA September OMR)

bullets.text: The White House signed H.R. 5334, the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, into law September 18, 2026, expanding sanctions and tariff authority relating to Russia and Iran and the shadow tanker system supporting Russian energy exports.

Brent closed the September 21-25 trading week at about $105.40 a barrel, up roughly 1.4 percent on the week, while WTI fell about 3.3 percent to roughly $92.90, as Houthi strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities and stop-start US-Iran negotiations pulled the two benchmarks in different directions.

Brent settled at $104.32 a barrel on September 25, down 2.1 percent, with WTI at $92.41, down 2.3 percent, as Iran's seven-day Hormuz proposal landed and the market priced a possible short-term thaw in Gulf shipping.

VLCC rates on West Asia–China routes hit a record $1.2 million a day, more than doubling since late August; Energy Aspects' Amrita Sen warned surging shipping costs could push delivered crude in Asia toward $150 a barrel.

The Baltic VLCC time-charter average rose from ~$198,000/day in July to ~$449,000/day in the first half of September, reaching ~$722,946/day by September 18, 2026, versus ~$79,700/day in mid-September 2025.

War-risk insurance premiums were revised from peacetime levels of 0.5–1% of hull and machinery value to approximately 10%, millions of dollars in added cost per VLCC voyage, passed through to charterers.
US Gulf–China VLCC rates were reported at $400,000 per day and Middle East Gulf spot rates at $1.25 million per day in late September 2026.

IEA projects 2026 world oil supply averaging 100.7 million b/d, down 5.7 million b/d year-on-year, with full recovery of Middle East supplies deferred until 2027; global oil demand is forecast to fall 2.5 million b/d in 2026.

Whether the Sep 22 LNG tanker strike is independently confirmed beyond UKMTO/DPA reporting.
EIA's next scheduled World Oil Transit Chokepoints update date was not found.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Fox News that Hormuz flows were averaging almost 13 million b/d with a single day above 20 million; single-outlet report, not corroborated against tracker data, so it is not used in the table.

watches.title: Iran watch
watches.dek: Iranian oil exports under sanctions and naval blockade: tanker-tracked export estimates, floating storage, grades and rerouting, the shadow fleet, and China's buying. Every figure carries its vintage.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the sanctioned sour barrel: Iran's exports are the largest single pool of distressed medium and heavy sour crude, and every number here is either tracker-observed or claimed, never both. Bullets say which, so treat Iranian state media figures as claims and tanker-tracker figures as observations.
watches.wcs_stakes: Iran is the marginal sour barrel in Asia: its exports land in the same Chinese teapot refineries that buy the Urals and other grades competing with Western Canadian Select (WCS). When Iranian barrels are blocked, teapots bid up substitute sours and the whole sour complex firms, supporting Canadian differentials; when the blockade loosens and Iranian crude flows again, medium and heavy sours soften first. The floating storage stockpile is the leading indicator: it is supply that can move without a single new barrel being produced.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, watch the floating storage drawdown and the blockade line: they tell you how much Iranian sour is coming before any official announcement. A sustained return of Iranian barrels would pressure the medium and heavy sour grades that price off Urals first, and Canadian heavies would feel it at the margin. The Iran Light premium flipping from discount to premium shows how fast the sour complex reprices when barrels vanish.

bullets.text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on September 27 that Tehran's conditions remain unchanged and that only a negotiated solution can end the standoff, adding that mediators had not yet formally conveyed a US rejection; a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran will show no flexibility on uranium enrichment.

President Trump said on September 26 that he had rejected the seven-day proposal, which had conditioned reopening Hormuz on a region-wide ceasefire, release of about $12 billion in frozen assets, a waiver of oil sanctions and an end to the US naval blockade; the Wall Street Journal reported US officials expect airstrikes to resume after the November midterms.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi detailed a seven-day Hormuz reopening plan in private meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on September 25: hostilities would end on all fronts including Lebanon within seven days, the US would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen funds and waive oil sanctions, after which nuclear talks would resume. The White House said September 25 it was having positive and constructive conversations with mediators.
bullets.source: The Hindu BusinessLine (citing the Associated Press)

bullets.text: A senior Iranian official told Reuters on September 25 that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts the Hormuz proposal, and that the waterway would stay closed until all of Iran's conditions are met. Tehran would give no concessions on enriching uranium or shipping highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands. President Pezeshkian said he hopes for a deal before the November 3 midterm elections.
The current war was triggered February 28, 2026 by joint US and Israeli strikes on Iran; Iran responded by closing commercial access to Hormuz. The US blockaded Iranian ports from April 13.

The US blockade of Iranian ports started April 13, 2026; United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI) measures exports by vessels crossing the blockade line from the eastern point of Oman to the Iran-Pakistan border, exiting the Gulf of Oman, rather than by point of loading.

Mid-June 2026, the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MOU) took effect and the US lifted the naval blockade under a sanctions waiver; Iran exported roughly 50 million barrels in the following two weeks (~1.66 million b/d in June, per TankerTrackers), and Iran's parliament speaker put the post-blockade figure above 40 million barrels.
In the 26 days after the MOU signing, Iran exported more than 80 million barrels of crude and products, worth over $6 billion at prevailing prices, per TankerTrackers.

Between the June 14 MOU announcement and July 6, Iran exported roughly 55 million barrels valued above $4.5 billion; pre-war, a typical month was 47-50 million barrels (~$3.05B), so the waiver window generated ~47% more revenue in 22 days than a full pre-war month.
Washington restored the blockade on July 14, 2026; Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers identified no Iranian crude cargo vessel successfully transiting Hormuz to China after that date.
bullets.source: National Security Journal (citing Vortexa, Kpler, Reuters)

bullets.text: On September 22, 2026, TankerTrackers spotted the first Iranian crude exports in two months: very large crude carriers (VLCCs) Diona (IMO 9569695) and Hero2 (IMO 9362073) plus the Suezmax tanker Sonia I exiting past the blockade line at the east end of the Gulf of Oman; Kpler confirmed four Iran-linked tankers exiting the Gulf of Oman.

Vessel-tracking data showed Iranian crude and condensate loadings averaged just 220,000 to 260,000 b/d in August 2026, down from 1.7 to 2.0 million b/d a year earlier, an over-80 percent collapse. No confirmed Iranian crude cargoes have passed the enforcement line since the US blockade went back up in mid-July, and analysts estimate production could fall to 1.2 to 1.3 million b/d if the blockade holds, near domestic consumption levels.
Iran's seaborne oil exports were 587 million barrels in 2024 (+10.75% y/y); China took 533 million barrels, 91% of the total, up 24% from 2023.
Iran exported 666 million barrels in 2025 (+13.5% y/y), with China by far the largest buyer.
March 2026 loadings were ~2.0 million b/d; July fell to ~749 kb/d of crude and condensate; August loadings were only ~220-255 kb/d.
bullets.source: National Security Journal (citing Vortexa, Kpler, Reuters)

bullets.text: May 2026 exports by sea were just 2.01 million barrels vs 29.7 million in April (-93%); the May total was four Panamax/Handymax naphtha shipments to China plus limited liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Very large crude carrier (VLCC) 2-million-barrel crude shipments dropped to zero.

Iran's pre-war baseline exports were 1.68 million b/d; TankerTrackers estimated they had fallen to zero by early September 2026 and could remain there 'for the foreseeable future' depending on any agreement.

Iranian state media claimed August 2026 oil exports above $3 billion, the highest monthly figure in two years, sharply at odds with tracker estimates of ~220-255 kb/d loaded that month; treat as claimed, not tracked.
Iranian floating crude was ~29 million barrels on September 8, 2026, down from ~90 million in mid-July, the blockade drew down pre-war floating stock by roughly two-thirds (Kpler, via WSJ).
bullets.source: WSJ via Kpler (compiled in Oil Depletion Report)

bullets.text: Vortexa's broader measure, all Iranian crude stored aboard tankers, fell from ~135 million barrels at end-July to ~107 million by August 26; Iran is drawing down crude that had already cleared the blockade without replacing it.
Iran sold about 9 million barrels (~$900M) out of floating storage in the Gulf of Oman, vessels already clear of Iranian ports when enforcement began, hence outside the blockade's reach.

TankerTrackers estimated ~30 million barrels of Iranian crude awaiting export in mid-July, with ~60 million barrels of floating storage capacity available in surrounding waters as a buffer if production faced restrictions.

sections.heading: What grades are stuck, and what unwinds first

bullets.text: Iran's export stream is medium and heavy sour crude: Iran Light (medium sour, American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity 33.6, 1.46% sulfur) and Iran Heavy (heavy sour, API gravity about 29.5, sulfur about 1.77%), per National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) assays reported by S&P Global Platts.
bullets.source: Hellenic Shipping News (citing S&P Global Platts)

bullets.text: China's independent refiners buy mainly Iran Light and some Iran Heavy. They crack Iran Light directly in their crude distillation units; Iran Heavy has to be blended with lighter grades first.

Iran Light is a direct substitute for Russian Urals in China's teapot refineries (independent refiners): similar medium sour specs (Iran Light 33.6 API and 1.46% sulfur vs Urals 31.7 API and 1.19%), and teapot sources say Iranian barrels suit their units better than Russian ones.

Scarcity is already pricing in: Kpler reported Iran Light flipping from a $3.50 per barrel discount to a $3.50 premium over Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent within a week as available floating cargoes thinned.

Kpler put total Iranian crude outside the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman at about 83 million barrels, with about 40 million at Singapore's Eastern Outer Port Limits (EOPL) anchorage, but only about 4 million barrels of that still unsold. An unwind would mostly deliver already-sold cargoes, not flood the spot market.

The reroute path back is Kharg Island loadings, transit through the Gulf of Oman, ship-to-ship transfer at EOPL Malaysia, delivery to Shandong teapots. Kpler notes teapots have been substituting Russian Urals and fuel oil while Iranian barrels were blocked, with the Eastern Siberia-Pacific Ocean (ESPO) blend sold out weeks in advance.

So the grades hit hardest by a return are medium and heavy sours: Russian Urals first (direct teapot substitute), then the wider medium-sour complex. Light sweets are less exposed, though record ESPO premiums of $20 to $30 per barrel over Brent would also ease.

No fresh sanctions designations on shadow-fleet vessels or entities appeared from the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control, the European Union, the United Kingdom, or the United Nations in the past week, per sanctions tracker Eagle Intelligence, leaving the enforcement picture flat even as Hormuz tensions raised tanker insurance costs.

Tracking data showed the tankers Tifani and Majestic X, seized by US forces in April, sailing along Brazil's northern coast while the June-seized Lenore rounded the Cape of Good Hope into the Atlantic, carrying nearly 6 million barrels of Iranian crude worth about $600 million toward the United States for expected forfeiture.

Bloomberg reported that the seized tankers Tiffany and Majestic X, both carrying Iranian crude, were tracked sailing along the Brazilian coast over the past week and are most likely headed for the United States, after several course changes since their seizure by US forces in April. The tanker Lenore, seized in the Indian Ocean in June, was spotted rounding the Cape of Good Hope west across the Atlantic; the combined cargo value of the three could reach $600 million.
UANI's 'ghost armada' reached 560 tracked tankers at end-2025 after 83 new vessels were identified during the year; of 180 tankers sanctioned in 2025, 108 had been previously identified by UANI.

TankerTrackers identified two US-sanctioned tankers in ballast that penetrated the blockade inbound for Iran with Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders on; the US Navy claims 13 Iranian tankers have been turned back so far.

During the June waiver window, 30+ tankers carrying 50M+ barrels of Iranian crude headed for Asia (Kpler); UANI separately tracked ~15 large Iranian-registered tankers departing Iranian ports with Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders switched on, a break from dark-fleet practice. For years, cargoes were masked via ship-to-ship (STS) transfers at Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits (EOPL) before continuing to Asia.

Treasury Secretary Bessent said the US sent warning letters to banks in China, Hong Kong, the UAE and Oman over continued Iranian-oil business, threatening secondary sanctions, 'the financial equivalent of a bomb' on Iran's oil sales system.

sections.heading: China: the buyer of last resort

bullets.text: China imported ~431 million barrels of Iranian oil in 2023 (over 80% of Iran's exports), rising to ~533 million in 2024 (over 91%), largely via ghost-fleet tankers offloading through intermediaries before reaching China.
bullets.source: Claire Jungman, UANI (House Foreign Affairs testimony)

bullets.text: Treasury Secretary Bessent said June 29, 2026 that despite the US lifting sanctions on Iranian oil, no country except China had bought at a discount, others held back fearing sanctions snapback.

China is expected to remain the biggest buyer via independent refiners; UANI's Charlie Brown noted it was unclear whether exporters would abandon the established EOPL ship-to-ship transfer networks even under the waiver.

gaps: Kpler and Vortexa publish different floating-storage scopes (Kpler ~29M bbl of floating crude Sep 8 vs Vortexa ~107M bbl of crude aboard tankers Aug 26); the two are not directly comparable, definitional difference, not a data conflict.
Iranian state media claimed August 2026 exports above $3B, a two-year high, while Vortexa/Kpler tracked only ~220-255 kb/d loaded that month, claimed vs tracked, unresolved.
The exact count of sanctioned vessels laden vs in ballast changes daily; no public source publishes it continuously.

watches.title: Red Sea Watch
watches.dek: Houthi pressure on Red Sea shipping: Bab el-Mandeb transit, territorial control, and the Cape of Good Hope diversion.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the routing risk behind the sour price: the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb decide whether Gulf crude reaches Europe and Asia on time or diverts around the Cape of Good Hope at record freight. Houthi claims are carried as claims, not confirmed incidents, and each bullet says which. Vessel counts are proxies for volume, and the quarterly official series lags.
watches.wcs_stakes: The Red Sea is the back door for Gulf sour barrels to Europe and the long way around to Asia, so its closure pushes those barrels onto longer routes at record freight and pushes European refiners onto substitute sours. That substitution is what keeps the bid under Atlantic Basin heavies like Mars and Western Canadian Select (WCS) while Yanbu loadings are suspended. If the East-West pipeline restart holds and Bab el-Mandeb transits recover, European sour demand normalizes and the support under WCS fades.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, the Red Sea is freight and substitution: watch Bab el-Mandeb transit counts and Yanbu loading resumption for the earliest sign that Gulf sour is reaching Europe normally again. While the reroute persists, record very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates keep delivered sour expensive and Canadian barrels relatively bid. The pipeline restart is fragile, so treat the recovery as a signal, not a settlement.

bullets.text: Kpler data showed commodity-vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb fell to 11 on September 27, the lowest level in months, as Red Sea traffic slowed after Houthi attacks on Saudi coastal installations, though two very large crude carriers were still inbound to Yanbu to load crude.

Saudi authorities ordered Riyadh schools to switch to remote learning for a week after Saudi air defenses said they intercepted Houthi drones aimed at the capital and ballistic missiles targeting Khamis Mushait; a Houthi political bureau member described the raid as a small-scale rehearsal for a full escalation.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck Aramco sites in Jizan and Yanbu on September 26, a claim Riyadh did not confirm; Kpler data showed only 11 commodity vessels transited Bab el-Mandeb on September 27, the lowest in months, though two very large crude carriers were still sailing to Yanbu to load Saudi crude.

Yemen's Houthi rebels captured the island of Mayun at the entrance of the Red Sea on September 25, a key position over the alternative shipping lane for Saudi oil while Hormuz is disrupted; Saudi Arabia responded with airstrikes against the airport in Mokha, the Red Sea port the Houthis seized the day before.

The Houthis claimed missile and drone attacks on September 24 against Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and a sensitive target in Riyadh; Saudi forces said they intercepted six ballistic missiles, with no damage confirmed by authorities.

The US Maritime Administration, in guidance effective September 23, urged US-flagged commercial vessels to switch off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) when transiting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, and to vary routes and speeds and limit electronic transmissions, as Houthi attacks persist. Vessels with links to Israel, the US, the UK or Saudi Arabia are considered at greater risk.

Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West Pipeline (Petroline) on September 22, 2026 after a nine-day shutdown triggered by drone attacks on September 13, with the line pumping at a low rate and Saudi Aramco seeking to return toward about 4 million barrels per day, roughly 4% of global oil supply; one crude cargo was scheduled to load at Yanbu later that Tuesday bound for China, and the restart pressured Brent crude futures down more than $2 a barrel to their lowest since September 8.

Before the attack, the East-West Pipeline carried roughly 5.5 million barrels per day, of which about 4.5 million barrels per day of crude was exported through Yanbu to Mediterranean and northwest European refiners without routing through the Strait of Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb; Houthi forces struck multiple pumping stations across two regions of Saudi Arabia on September 10, no crude has loaded from Yanbu since September 11, and terminal inventories were estimated to cover only three to five days of loadings at normal rates.

The Houthis claimed on September 23 that they struck the Saudi oil tanker Wafa with ballistic missiles off the coast of Yanbu, calling the strike precise but giving no details of damage or casualties; the claim was not independently verified and Saudi authorities did not immediately respond. The Houthi spokesperson also claimed eight Saudi oil tankers have been targeted since the campaign began with 29 others forced to turn back, figures that are self-reported.

The Houthis said they targeted the Saudi oil tanker Amzan in the Red Sea off Yanbu with a ballistic missile and drones earlier in the week; unlike the later claims, this incident drew confirmation from the Saudi side, with Saudi shipping company Bahri stating its Amzan vessel was involved in a hostile incident in regional waters.

Traffic through Bab el-Mandeb stayed volatile but open: 22 commodity vessels crossed on Tuesday, September 22 (14 toward the Red Sea, 8 toward the Gulf of Aden), below the 10-day average of about 26 but well above the single-digit levels seen through the Strait of Hormuz over the same weekend.

Brent rose more than 3 percent on September 24, briefly topping $108 a barrel, before easing to $105.77 on September 25 morning, as Houthi strikes on Yanbu added pressure on Saudi Arabia's oil exports; analysts said crude would likely stay above $100 a barrel as long as the war on Iran continued.

With Yanbu loadings suspended, Saudi Aramco cancelled or delayed some September crude cargoes to European refiners, which may need to source alternative barrels from the Americas, the North Sea, and Africa at higher freight costs; Kpler estimates cited at the time put Yanbu inventories below 15 million barrels, enough for only about four days of exports at 3.5 million barrels per day.

The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) reported that 5,874 vessels carrying 247.2 million tons transited the canal from July through mid-September 2026, generating $1.97 billion in revenue, up 5.2% in vessel count, 14.4% in tonnage, and 17.5% in revenue versus the same period last year; chairman Ossama Rabiee also projected canal revenue reaching about $8 billion in fiscal year 2026/27.
bullets.source: State Information Service Egypt (quoting the Suez Canal Authority)

bullets.text: COSCO Shipping Lines made its first southbound Suez transit since the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb tensions disrupted patterns, with the 24,188 twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU) OOCL Portugal sailing from Belgium to China on September 16; the Suez Canal Authority (SCA) said container-ship net tonnage through the canal reached about 72.1 million tonnes in January-August 2026, up 54.2% year on year, and that services by CMA CGM, Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), Hapag-Lloyd, and COSCO have returned to the canal on Europe-Asia trades.
bullets.source: Container News (citing the Suez Canal Authority)

bullets.text: War-risk pricing has split into tiers rather than one Red Sea number: indicative premiums for the southern Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb rose above 1% of vessel value from about 0.3% a week earlier, Saudi-linked voyages were quoted as high as 3%, while the northern Saudi Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Yanbu were quoted around 0.1%, a markedly different near-term risk profile.

Xeneta analyst Peter Sand said ocean freight is unlikely to return to Suez at scale for the rest of 2026, warning that renewed Houthi attacks would shelve any phased return; he estimates the Cape of Good Hope routing absorbs about 2.5 million TEU of the global 34 million TEU boxship fleet, shrinking available capacity by roughly 7%. Separately, leading protection and indemnity (P&I) clubs and their reinsurers are pulling war-risk cover for much of the Gulf region, effectively putting the Arabian Gulf off-limits for insurance purposes.

Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan arrived in Washington on September 28 for talks with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as Riyadh seeks US help against the Houthis; Reuters sources said Washington agreed to intelligence and targeting support while declining to launch strikes itself.

Military chiefs from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met in Riyadh under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement to review the threats facing the kingdom, condemning Houthi attacks and agreeing to deepen intelligence sharing and military coordination.

France confirmed on September 25 it will send troops, radars and air-defense systems to guard the oil terminal at Yanbu; separately, the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey arranged an urgent meeting of military chiefs under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all.

Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said early on September 26 it intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom, the missiles headed for Khamis Mushait and the drones for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia's military chiefs met in Riyadh with allies Pakistan and Turkey to review threats.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on September 21 that Britain would provide limited military support to Saudi Arabia, with the Royal Air Force (RAF) supplying defensive air-to-air refueling for Saudi aircraft on missions countering Houthi missile and drone attacks; the agreement runs for a matter of weeks and will be kept under review. The United States, which bombed the Houthis under the Biden and Trump administrations, has shown no interest in getting involved militarily this time.

Weekly transit volume through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait grew from 1.1 million to 1.5 million metric tons (roughly 32 to 38 vessel transits) between January and July 2026 as Hormuz disruption pushed traffic south, but contracted to 25 weekly transits carrying about 750,000 metric tons after Houthi missile strikes resumed in July; for scale, pre-October 2023 traffic averaged about 80 vessels and 3.4 million metric tons per week, so Red Sea shipping is still below a third of its old normal.
bullets.vintage: Data: Jan-Jul 2026 and pre-2023 baseline; accessed 2026-09-24

gaps: No single verified series for daily Bab el-Mandeb oil volume in September 2026, trackers report vessel counts, EIA reports quarterly volumes with a lag.
Houthi merchant-ship count claims (408 ships Sep 11–21) are self-reported and not independently verified.
Exact per-route freight surcharge pass-through to delivered crude prices is estimated, not measured.
No verified current count of how many Houthi attacks on vessels have occurred in 2026 specifically targeting tankers vs other shipping.
No independent confirmation of Houthi tanker-hit claims (Wafa, Amzan) or the claimed tally of eight Saudi tankers struck and 29 turned back.
Repair timeline for the East-West Pipeline pumping stations is unverified; estimates range from weeks to six-plus weeks and the effective restart rate is unknown.
No public breakdown of where Saudi Gulf-terminal loadings went during the Petroline outage, limiting the Europe-vs-Asia crude split read.

watches.title: Russian Refining Watch
watches.dek: Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refining: strikes, offline capacity, and the diesel crisis.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the diesel side of the crude market: Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries remove products, not crude, so the read is crack spreads and export curbs rather than wellhead output. Ukrainian claims are carried as claims. Strike dates are approximate and every bullet carries its vintage.
watches.wcs_stakes: Russian refinery outages tighten global diesel, and record diesel cracks keep US and Asian refiners running at maximum to capture them, which is the demand-side bid under heavy sour barrels including Western Canadian Select (WCS). At the same time, crude displaced from downed Russian refineries has pushed seaborne Russian exports to 16-month highs, capping how much support the tight product market can pass back to sour crude prices. The net effect for WCS is constructive while diesel cracks stay extreme: refineries run hard and bid for every discounted heavy barrel they can crack.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, watch the diesel crack, not the strike count: it is the margin that decides how hard refiners run and how much they pay for heavy barrels. If an energy ceasefire returns Russian refineries and the diesel crack compresses, runs fall and discounted heavies strand first. Until then, the tight product market is the best demand cover WCS has.

bullets.text: Bloomberg tanker-tracking data cited by OilPrice.com show Russia's seaborne crude exports averaged 3.62 million barrels per day in the four weeks to September 28, the highest since May 2024, a sign that neither India nor other major buyers have reduced purchases despite US pressure. Russia's oil and gas revenues were nevertheless expected to plunge 23 percent year on year in September on lower crude prices and a stronger ruble, per Reuters calculations cited in the piece.
bullets.vintage: Data: four weeks ending Sep 28, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24

bullets.text: The Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, the main western outlet for displaced crude, is itself constrained: trader data show exports and transit volumes more than halved from July to August, from 800,000 barrels per day to less than 355,000, after repeated drone strikes collapsed loadings and thinned tanker availability. Chartering a Suezmax tanker to India from Novorossiysk cost about $20 million by the end of August, versus about $13 million a month earlier.

President Trump said he asked President Zelenskyy to reduce strikes on Russian oil refineries, warning they could create a global problem, and claimed Zelenskyy said he probably would, though Kyiv did not confirm that response.

Both sides kept striking energy assets despite Trump's September 14 announcement of a mutual pledge to stop; Zelenskyy said Kyiv is ready for an energy ceasefire and floated US-pushed trilateral technical talks possibly in Abu Dhabi, while Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Putin and Trump discussed such a meeting but gave no specifics.

Russia's seaborne oil product exports rebounded 16.4 percent from July in August to 4.57 million metric tons as some refineries returned from unplanned maintenance, but remained 50 percent below August 2025. The mix skewed to naphtha and fuel oil, Baltic shipments rose 32.7 percent while Black Sea and Azov Sea loadings fell 25.3 percent. Russian diesel exports had already fallen below 1 million metric tons in June, versus roughly 2.5 million tons per month a year earlier. Moscow is extending its diesel export ban through October 31, according to Russian media reports, to rebuild stocks before winter.
bullets.source: OilPrice.com (citing industry sources and Reuters calculations)

bullets.text: The Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) gasoil crack hit a record $79 per barrel in early September, with the U.S. diesel crack trading above $100 per barrel near all-time highs and the September-November gasoil spread at an $80-per-metric-ton backwardation, according to ING (Internationale Nederlanden Groep) commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey. They expect middle-distillate cracks to stay elevated and volatile into seasonally stronger demand, warning the global refining system has little slack to make up for lost Middle Eastern and Russian flows.

After the September 20 Moscow refinery strike, Bloomberg data showed the U.S. heating-oil crack spread hit an all-time high of $117 per barrel, the highest since the series began in 2009, and U.S. retail diesel rose to a record $6.45 per gallon, its first move above $6.00. Shortages have already surfaced at filling stations in rural Brazil, Libya and parts of Africa, where diesel powers trucking, farming and backup generation. 'We are witnessing what may be the tightest diesel market structure in history,' said David Martin, senior oil market analyst at the International Energy Agency (IEA).

President Trump wrote on Truth Social on September 21 that 'Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,' adding that 'a large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up' and are 'at least temporarily, out of commission.' The day before, the Financial Times (FT) reported Trump phoned Zelenskyy to press him to halt refinery strikes; a senior Ukrainian official on the call said Trump's message was 'diesel, diesel, diesel,' and a second official said Trump wants Russian fuel back on the world market to push prices down.

Trump and Zelenskyy held a 40-minute meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on September 22 that produced no announced terms, no monitoring system and no Russian commitment on an energy ceasefire; Zelenskyy said Washington would convey the proposal to Moscow. Afterward Zelenskyy told reporters Ukraine was ready for 'any format' of a reciprocal energy ceasefire and said Trump had not asked Kyiv to halt refinery strikes unilaterally.

Zelenskyy said after the September 22 United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) meeting that Ukraine is ready for an energy ceasefire if Russia does not attack Ukraine's energy, electricity, heating and water systems, and he asked Trump to organize a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying leaders must move 'as quickly as possible' to end the war. A winter package of Patriot air-defense missiles and licenses to produce them domestically were two of Kyiv's priorities for the coming months, Zelenskyy said. NPR national security correspondent Greg Myre framed the winter urgency: 'We have to prepare for the winter. And if it will be winter in war, it will be not simple.'

European gasoil cracks to Brent hit record highs around September 23, driven by fears of possible U.S. diesel export restrictions and structural shortfalls in global refining, alongside persistent outages at refineries in Russia and parts of the Middle East. The Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) gasoil October contract rose nearly $72 per metric ton on September 23 alone. The tightness is now the main support for prompt crude prices: the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) November 2026 to December 2028 spread exceeded $23 per barrel, a steep backwardation.

Ukraine launched a large overnight drone attack on fuel depots in Russia's Krasnodar region, with local authorities reporting fires at three sites and no casualties in Krasnodar, while Russia's Defense Ministry claimed 254 Ukrainian drones were shot down across 15 regions, a figure that was not independently confirmed.

Ukrainian drones struck the Afipsky oil refinery in Krasnodar region, starting a fire, and hit Port Kavkaz on the Kerch Strait, injuring three people and damaging a service vessel and the pier complex, according to local authorities.

Ukraine struck the Ilsky refinery in Krasnodar region overnight on September 26, damaging the AT-4, AT-5 and AT-6 primary units, about 99 percent of its primary capacity, and the plant halted production; Ukraine's General Staff confirmed the strike and the regional governor confirmed drone attacks in the Seversky district.
bullets.source: Meanwhile in Ukraine (citing Ukraine's General Staff)

bullets.text: Ukraine struck the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez refinery, Russia's seventh-largest at about 252,000 b/d in 2024, on the night of September 24 into 25; geolocated footage showed a drone hitting the AVT-5 crude unit, roughly 34 percent of capacity. Reuters reported on September 26 that the refinery stopped operations after the attack damaged pipelines, storage and processing units. The plant sits more than 1,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.

The Novoshakhtinsk refinery in Russia's Rostov region was damaged overnight September 24 to 25 and temporarily suspended operations, Governor Yuri Slyusar said; Russia's defense ministry said air defenses destroyed 592 drones overnight. One man was killed in the Perm region during the same wave.

The Ilsky refinery in Krasnodar Krai was reportedly struck on September 26, making it the fourth Russian refinery to suspend operations in less than a week amid the sustained Ukrainian campaign against oil-processing infrastructure.

Ukraine expanded the campaign from refineries to crude logistics around September 20-21: drones hit the Lazarevo pumping station in the Kirov region, about 1,300 kilometers from Ukrainian-held territory, which serves the Surgut-Gorky-Polotsk pipeline carrying Siberian crude to Belarus. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a fresh strike on the Saratov refinery that sparked a large fire, a fuel depot at Matveyev Kurgan in the Rostov region burned after a drone strike, and the Moscow-appointed governor of Crimea announced gasoline sales restrictions without giving a reason. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed 216 drones were intercepted; the damage assessments are unconfirmed.

Russia retaliated against Ukrainian energy targets around September 22-23: Russia's Defense Ministry claimed missile and rocket strikes on the Kremenchuk oil refinery, fuel storage near Kyiv, a solid rocket fuel plant in Pavlograd, a Kyiv factory it said makes components and warheads for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, plus railway and port infrastructure at Vinnytsia, Reni and Odesa. Ukrainian authorities had not issued a consolidated damage assessment, and there was no independent verification of the Russian claims.

Ukraine's Defense Intelligence representative Andrii Yusov said Ukrainian forces have conducted 64 targeted strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure facilities this year, destroying or damaging about one-third of the targeted refineries and storage facilities, and said the strikes compound Western sanctions that restrict imports of repair equipment. The agency framed the disruption as long-term pressure on Russian military logistics. This is a Ukrainian claim, not independently verified.

gaps: Russian government has not published confirmed damage figures; offline estimates are Western/industry estimates or Ukrainian claims.
Repair timelines reported by sources (weeks to months) are not independently verifiable.
Whether repair times are lengthening due to sanctions on replacement equipment could not be verified from a primary source.
No confirmed independent series for Russia's actual monthly refinery throughput in 2026 beyond IEA estimates.

No public reconciliation between the International Energy Agency's June throughput estimate (3.8 million barrels per day) and JPMorgan's current sub-5-million estimate; the two may use different definitions, and the gap matters for judging how fast capacity is being lost.

No public data on how much crude displaced from downed refineries is being rerouted to export terminals versus going into storage, or whether port and shadow-fleet tanker capacity cap the redirection.
Whether market talk of possible U.S. diesel export restrictions (flagged in commentary around September 23) reflects real policy discussion could not be verified from an official source.

watches.title: China Import Watch
watches.dek: China's crude buying: import volumes, sourcing shifts, teapot run rates, and what it means for sour barrel demand.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the buy side of the sour barrel: China's import volumes and refinery runs decide how much sour crude Asia pulls, and the stock math (imports plus domestic production minus throughput) shows whether Beijing is building inventories or drawing them. Every bullet carries its vintage, so read 2026 wartime figures against pre-war baselines rather than against last week alone.
watches.wcs_stakes: China's buying is rotating, not growing: Russian and Iranian crude fell below one-third of September imports from about half in August (Goldman Sachs), and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain on the water under the US blockade -- a forced shift toward non-sanctioned sour that bids up the grades Western Canadian Select (WCS) competes with. But the bid is selective: seaborne imports sit almost 3 million b/d below normal seasonal levels even as refineries processed 13.91 million b/d in August, the most since March. Watch the Kayrros satellite inventory reads and the monthly throughput numbers: restocking bids up sour, stock draws soften the WCS basis.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, China matters through the sour barrel, not through direct Canadian sales. Strong Chinese runs and restocking bid up the grades Mars and Urals price against, which keeps the Canadian differential tight; a stock draw and a buying pause do the opposite. The teapot substitution story, Urals and fuel oil standing in for blocked Iranian barrels, is the near-term variable to watch.

bullets.text: Goldman Sachs estimated China's seaborne crude net imports rose about 6 percent in September from August but stayed almost 3 million barrels per day below normal seasonal levels, and its models point to only about 600,000 barrels per day more total crude imports in the fourth quarter versus the third. The bank estimates a sustained 1 million barrel per day change in China's net crude imports over six months would shift Brent's fair value by about 4 dollars a barrel.

Reuters columnist Clyde Russell's analysis of official data (published Sep 15, 2026) showed China processed 13.91 million b/d in August, the most since March, against 8.93 million b/d of imports plus 4.34 million b/d of domestic production, implying a 640,000 b/d inventory draw. It was the third draw in four months (draws of 500,000 b/d in May and 940,000 b/d in June, a 210,000 b/d surplus in July); stocks are estimated at at least 1.2 billion barrels, and January to August still showed a net surplus of 330,000 b/d.

Kpler data cited by Maritime Professional (Sep 23, 2026) put Asia on course to import 23.96 million b/d of crude in September, up from 23.38 million in August and the highest since February, extending the recovery from April's decade-plus low. Even so, September remained 13% below the 27.55 million b/d three-month pre-conflict average through February.
bullets.vintage: Prelim data: Sep 2026; published Sep 23, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24

bullets.text: Russian and Iranian crude accounted for less than one-third of China's September imports, down from about half in August, as China shifted toward non-sanctioned supply, per Goldman Sachs analysis. The bank said the shift toward openly traded crude could make changes in Chinese purchasing more visible in benchmark pricing.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Fox News interview on Sep 27 that only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain on the water under the US blockade, with final deliveries to China expected within about two weeks, after which he claimed Iran would have nothing left to trade. That is an unverified prediction from the official directing the sanctions effort, not independent evidence that Iranian exports have stopped.

TankerTrackers reported Sep 24 that almost 6 million barrels of confiscated Iranian crude, including the 1.88-million-barrel tanker Majestic X seized in the Indian Ocean in April while headed for China, were crossing the Atlantic toward the United States. The report relies on a single tracking source and should be treated as a lead until corroborated.
bullets.vintage: TankerTrackers report Sep 24, 2026; published Sep 26, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: Saudi Aramco cut its September official selling price (OSP) for Arab Light to Asia by 50 cents a barrel to a $2/bbl discount against the regional benchmark, the fifth-lowest differential since 2000, per Energies Media (Aug 19, 2026). The cut reflected war-driven costs (freight, rerouting) plus formal discount requests from Asian refiners for longer voyages; Aramco held exports near 5 million b/d, about 70% of normal, leaning on Red Sea port Yanbu and potentially Sidi Kerir loadings.

Saudi Arabia left its October-loading Arab Light official selling price (OSP) to Asia unchanged, according to Reuters reporting via TradingView on Sep 3, 2026, pausing the easing that had taken the September price to a $2/bbl discount against the regional benchmark.

Gasoline inventories at state-owned majors fell 2.9 percent in a week to their lowest since 2022 and diesel stocks hit a 15-month low after a 2.4 percent drop, per commodity research firm JLC International cited by Bloomberg. Energy Aspects analyst Jiana Sun told Bloomberg there is a growing risk Beijing caps monthly clean product exports at about 1.2 million tons in the fourth quarter.

Energy News Beat (Sep 13, 2026) reported the second batch of 2026 clean-product export quotas brought China's total 2026 allocation to about 32 million tonnes. August product exports hit 6.01 million tonnes, up 12.7% year on year, but January to August exports were still down 9.6% year on year, with gasoline down 57% year to date, consistent with a policy-managed surplus rather than an unconstrained export boom.

General Administration of Customs (GAC) data reported by IDNFinancials (Sep 18, 2026) gave August per-fuel detail: gasoline exports 700,000 tonnes, down 17.5% year on year but the highest since October 2025; diesel 1.33 million tonnes, up 42.1% year on year and the highest since March 2024; jet fuel a record 2.55 million tonnes, up 41.4% year on year. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports fell 17.8% year on year to 5.16 million tonnes.

Baird Maritime (Sep 21, 2026, citing GAC customs data) reported China's August fuel oil exports fell to 1.21 million tonnes (about 247,000 b/d), down 35% month on month and 27% year on year, the lowest since October 2024, partly on weather disruption at the Zhoushan bunkering hub. Fuel oil imports were 1.3 million tonnes, up 15% month on month and down 11% year on year; crude throughput climbed for a second month, supported by stronger fuel exports after Beijing eased export restrictions in mid-July.

Baltic Exchange data put the time charter equivalent for a 270,000-ton very large crude carrier (VLCC) on the TD3C Middle East Gulf to China route at about 1.212 million dollars per day on Sep 17, up from about 1.034 million the day before and roughly 700,000 at the start of September. The Baltic's Sep 18 weekly report put TD3C at Worldscale 1,140, the Gulf of Oman to China TD34 route at 870,947 dollars per day, and West Africa to China TD15 at 524,575 dollars per day.

The 2016-built VLCC Kuwait Prosperity, operated by Sinokor, was fixed at Worldscale 1,350 for a Persian Gulf to east voyage loading by Total Singapore on Sep 22, with a daily equivalent estimated above 1 million dollars. Analysts attribute the spike to reduced Hormuz transits, longer voyages via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, and diversions around the Cape of Good Hope adding an estimated 11 to 14 million dollars per voyage in charter costs alone.
bullets.vintage: Fixture for Sep 22 loading; reported Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: Tide Signal News (Sep 23, 2026, citing Reuters/Baltic Exchange data) reported very large crude carrier (VLCC) freight from the Gulf of Oman to China hit Worldscale 450, about $11.50 per barrel, a record for the route and up roughly 65% from the Sep 4 TD34 assessment, as conflict risk shrank the pool of tankers willing to trade around the Gulf.

Vessel Hunter News (Sep 22, 2026, citing Baltic Exchange data) reported the TD3C Middle East Gulf to China very large crude carrier (VLCC) time-charter equivalent reached $1.2125 million a day on Sep 17, up 40.6% on the week and roughly ten times the $117,400 a day before the February conflict. TD15 West Africa to Far East hit $524,500 a day and TD22 US Gulf to Far East $388,400 a day; the China Crude Oil Tanker Freight Index stood at 14,575 points on Sep 16, about 83% above its early-September level.
bullets.source: Vessel Hunter News (citing Baltic Exchange data)

bullets.text: The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air's August 2026 snapshot (published Sep 17, 2026) found refinery throughput down 6.9% year on year in August, though recovered from July's slump. New energy vehicle (NEV) output rose 21.9% year on year to 61% of all vehicles produced, and battery production surged 70% year on year, consistent with continued structural gasoline displacement.
bullets.source: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air

bullets.text: The US Energy Information Administration (EIA), in analysis published April 2026, classifies China's strategic oil inventories at an estimated 1.397 billion barrels, comprising about 360 million barrels government-held and 1 billion barrels commercial. The EIA treats both as strategic because China's national oil companies have reportedly been instructed since 2024 to hold emergency oil in commercial tanks.

Geospatial firm Kayrros, via MEXC reporting from the Asia Pacific Petroleum Conference (APPEC) in Singapore, estimated China's strategic petroleum reserve (SPR) at about 415 million barrels and commercial stocks at about 780 million barrels in early September 2026, up close to 130 million barrels combined since late March, with above-ground capacity use near 60.5%, leaving room for further builds.
bullets.vintage: Estimate: early Sep 2026; reported from APPEC; accessed 2026-09-24
bullets.source: MEXC (citing Kayrros chief analyst Antoine Halff at APPEC)

gaps: No single authoritative public series for China's SPR (strategic) inventory changes, estimates rely on satellite/stock-model data.
Current (September 2026) teapot run rates rely on consultancy surveys (Mysteel, JLC, Oilchem) rather than official NBS data, which lags.
Vintage of the exact Russian ESPO/Urals spot premiums could not be fully reconciled across sources; treat as reported.
Whether China's fuel export controls will tighten or loosen further after September is not verifiable.
Whether Beijing issues a third batch of 2026 crude import quotas for independent refiners in Q4, and how much of the 257Mt annual allocation remains unreleased.

No public time series for tank fill levels at new strategic reserve sites; satellite estimates (Kayrros) remain the only near-real-time read, and government vs commercial split is an EIA assumption, not disclosed data.
Aramco's November 2026 official selling prices to Asia (expected around Oct 5) will set the trend for Iranian, Kuwaiti and Iraqi differentials into Q4; direction not verifiable until release.

watches.title: US SPR & Storage Watch
watches.dek: US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and commercial crude stocks -- SPR inventory, the 2026 exchange/refill mechanics, and Cushing.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the US government's sour barrel: the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is mostly sour crude, and its exchanges put barrels into the market while the returns schedule takes them back out. The reserve's published inventory is the hard data; the 2026 exchange repayment ledger is not published, so outstanding loan balances are estimates. Every bullet carries its vintage.
watches.wcs_stakes: What's drawing lately is leaning sweet: between August 20 and September 11 the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) lost 5.0 million barrels of sweet against 4.2 million of sour, leaving it at roughly 34% sweet and 66% sour against the 40/60 mix the Department of Energy (DOE) says US Gulf Coast refineries were built around, and at 284.9 million barrels the reserve sits only about 32 million above the 252.4-million-barrel minimum Congress mandates. Near term the pressure stays bearish: Energy Secretary Chris Wright calls another exchange round 'a very real possibility' with 38.5 million barrels still unallocated. The trade flips in 2027, when borrowers start returning barrels at about 1.25 per barrel borrowed through 2029, turning the SPR from the market's biggest sour supplier into a standing bid for medium-sour crude.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, the SPR is a two-act story with a grade twist: exchanges now, repayments later, and sweet leaving fastest while the reserve drifts further from its 40/60 design mix. Watch the weekly EIA petroleum status report for the draw pace, the DOE grade table for the sweet/sour split, and any disclosed repayments; the 2027-2029 return schedule is a known future bid for sour barrels. Until then, the reserve's releases are the quiet headwind on every sour differential print, and the 252.4-million-barrel congressional floor leaves only about 32 million barrels of drawdown room.

sections.heading: What's drawing lately: sweet vs sour

bullets.text: DOE's per-site grade table as of August 20, 2026 showed 101.8 million barrels of sweet and 192.3 million of sour (294.1 million total), or roughly 34.6% sweet and 65.4% sour. DOE defines sweet as sulfur content no greater than 0.5% by weight and sour as greater than 0.5% but less than 2.0%; DOE's stated design ratio is about 40% sweet to 60% sour, based on likely US refinery needs, especially on the Gulf Coast.
bullets.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts)

bullets.text: DOE reported the reserve at 284.9 million barrels as of September 11, split 96.8 million sweet and 188.1 million sour (Reuters). Against the August 20 DOE table, sweet drew about 5.0 million barrels and sour about 4.2 million over roughly three weeks, with sweet leaving slightly faster in absolute terms; the sweet share slipped to about 34.0%, drifting further from DOE's 40% design target. Note the September 11 split comes from secondary reporting of a DOE figure, not the published Quick Facts grade table.
bullets.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine)

bullets.text: The September 11 total sat about 32.5 million barrels above the 252.4-million-barrel minimum Congress mandates, so the exchange program has limited drawdown room left before hitting the statutory floor. DOE says it has secured cancellation of 140 million barrels of congressionally mandated sales scheduled for fiscal years 2024 through 2027, so there is no forced-sale overhang on the forward calendar.
bullets.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine); US Department of Energy (energy.gov)

bullets.text: Refill buying stays token: the Senate-passed July 2025 budget bill cut SPR crude purchase funding to $171 million from the House's $1.3 billion, roughly 3 million barrels at prevailing prices, and kept the repeal of the last 7 million barrels of congressionally mandated sales through fiscal year 2027 (final legislative status unconfirmed).

Near term the program still leans bearish for sour: Secretary Wright said in mid-September that another round of exchange loans is 'a very real possibility', with about 38.5 million barrels of the 172-million-barrel authorized program still unallocated. The reversal is scheduled: borrowed crude is expected to start returning early in 2027 and run through 2029 at roughly 1.25 barrels returned per barrel borrowed, implying about 35 to 40 million premium barrels on top of the principal that the market must supply back to the reserve.
bullets.source: Turkiye New Updates (citing Argus Media via Anadolu Agency); BOE Report (citing Reuters)

sections.heading: US petroleum stocks: crude, distillate, and gasoline

bullets.text: Commercial crude stocks rose 3.0 million barrels to 426.4 million barrels in the week ending September 18, roughly 2 percent above the five-year average, while analysts surveyed by Reuters had expected a 641,000-barrel draw. Crude at the Cushing, Oklahoma delivery hub rose 2.2 million barrels to 23.7 million barrels.
bullets.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 18, 2026; published Sep 23, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: The Energy Information Administration's (EIA) report for the week ending September 18, 2026 (released September 23) showed commercial crude stocks rising 3.0 million barrels to 426.4 million, about 2 percent above the five-year seasonal average, as refinery runs fell 2.8 percentage points to 94.0 percent and crude inputs dropped 519,000 b/d to 16.8 million b/d. Gasoline stocks fell 1.7 million barrels to 206 million (6 percent below the five-year average) and distillate stocks fell 428,000 barrels to 107.4 million (12 percent below); US crude production was 13.9 million b/d with imports of 5.9 million b/d and exports of 3.3 million b/d.

bullets.text: Cushing, Oklahoma (the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) delivery hub for West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures) built 2.3 million barrels in the September 18 week to 23.7 million barrels, an 11 percent jump after falling to 21.5 million the prior week.
