sections.heading: Distillate: the tightest buffer into winter

bullets.text: After Politico reported the White House was preparing a 90-day diesel export ban, the White House denied the report on Sep 23 while President Trump said he backed a ban; Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the same day that a ban would not work and could push up gasoline and jet fuel prices, pushing instead for voluntary refiner cooperation. US diesel futures fell 4 percent on the news, with the national average diesel price near 6.52 dollars a gallon per AAA.

Senators Susan Collins and Angus King of Maine wrote to President Trump on Sep 22 asking him to release home heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, noting Maine households are paying about 675 dollars more per tank fill than last year and diesel has surged past 6.50 dollars a gallon. The 1-million-barrel reserve, stored at four sites from Maine to New Jersey, holds roughly 10 days of regional supply and has not been tapped since Hurricane Sandy in 2012.
bullets.vintage: Letter sent Sep 22, 2026; published Sep 23, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: Atlantic coast distillate inventories fell to 19.3 million barrels in the final week of August, the lowest weekly level since records began in 1990, recovering only to 21.6 million by September 11, while US distillate exports hit a record 1.88 million barrels per day in late July. Canada's 320,000-barrel-per-day Saint John refinery, a major supplier of ultra low sulfur diesel to the northeastern US, is undergoing a 75-day maintenance program from early September to mid-November.

Distillate stocks (diesel and heating oil) were 107.4 million barrels in the week ending September 18, about 12 percent below the five-year seasonal average, and the US entered autumn with refiners near their ceiling: distillate production averaged 5.1 million b/d from January through August (the most since 2019) and utilization hit 97 to 98 percent in early September. Diesel averaged $6.52 per gallon (American Automobile Association) and heating oil traded near a record around $5 per gallon, roughly 120 percent above a year earlier, while net distillate exports sat near or above their 2021-2025 high since February and Russia planned to extend diesel export restrictions through October.
bullets.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 18, 2026; reported Sep 18-23, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24
bullets.source: Daily Caller News Foundation (citing EIA and AAA); TradingEconomics (citing EIA); The Autowire (citing EIA)

bullets.text: The Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve holds about one million barrels of heating oil, roughly five days of regional supply, and a release requires the heating-oil-over-crude price spread to run more than 60 percent above its five-year average for seven straight days while continuing to widen. Unlike the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), the Northeast reserve holds refined fuel that can go directly to heating-oil markets, but a price spike alone does not automatically trigger a release; it must meet the statutory dislocation standard (National Energy Assistance Directors Association).
bullets.source: Daily Caller News Foundation (quoting National Energy Assistance Directors Association)

bullets.text: The Energy Information Administration's (EIA) September Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) raised its 2026 distillate crack spread forecast to $1.57 per gallon, up 20.8 percent from the August estimate, and lifted the 2027 figure to $1.25, formalizing the market's bet that refinery margins stay elevated while global middle-distillate balances stay tight. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, Russia's diesel export curbs, and Middle East supply risk are cited as the drivers.
bullets.vintage: EIA September 2026 STEO; reported Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24
bullets.source: The Autowire (citing EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook)

bullets.text: Energy Secretary Chris Wright clarified in a CNBC interview that Venezuela's heavy crude would not be placed directly into reserve salt caverns but could be swapped for light or medium US barrels, because much of Venezuela's oil is heavier and higher in sulfur than the crude traditionally held in the reserve. Analysts quoted in the piece cautioned that many of the Venezuelan fields would need years of development and reinvestment before producing meaningful volumes.

In June 2026 the Department of Energy (DOE) awarded contracts for a further approximately 53.3 million barrels of Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) exchange crude across all four sites (Bayou Choctaw, Bryan Mound, Big Hill, West Hackberry) under its late-April request for proposal, carrying an approximately 28 percent return premium (15.1 million barrels). DOE said about 35 million barrels had been delivered to market to that point and that earlier phases had awarded roughly 80 million barrels (45.2 plus 8.5 plus 26 million).

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in mid-September that the US has lent more than 130 million barrels (over three-quarters of the 172-million-barrel authorized exchange), with about 38.5 million barrels still unallocated and another round of loans 'a very real possibility' while front-month West Texas Intermediate (WTI) trades roughly 25 percent above the six-month contract. Borrowed crude is expected to start returning early in 2027 and continue through 2029 at roughly 1.25 barrels returned per barrel borrowed, implying about 35 to 40 million premium barrels on top of the principal.
bullets.source: Turkiye New Updates (citing Argus Media via Anadolu Agency); BOE Report (citing Reuters)

bullets.text: Other International Energy Agency (IEA) members' announced contributions to the 400-million-barrel coordinated release included 22.46 million barrels from South Korea and 13.5 million barrels from the United Kingdom, with Germany, Austria, and Japan also releasing stock (Japan's releases began in mid-March), per reporting in late July 2026. Aggregate member delivery progress beyond these pledges has not been published in a single authoritative ledger.

The reserve held 284.6 million barrels in the week ending September 18, down 29.9 percent from a year earlier and down 130.5 million barrels since reaching 415.1 million on March 27, leaving it at roughly 40 percent of its 714-million-barrel design capacity across four Gulf Coast sites.
bullets.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 18, 2026; published ~Sep 25, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: The Energy Information Administration (EIA) weekly series puts the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at its lowest weekly level since November 1982; Brookings Institution analyst Samantha Gross warned that aggressive pumping can damage the salt caverns themselves.

The Department of Energy's (DOE) Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) Quick Facts page put per-site inventory at 294.1 million barrels as of August 20, 2026: Bryan Mound 142.5 million (48 percent of the reserve), Big Hill 89.1 million, West Hackberry 30.5 million, and Bayou Choctaw 32.0 million. The quality split was 101.8 million barrels sweet and 192.3 million sour, meaning roughly 65 percent of the remaining reserve is sour crude.
bullets.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts)

bullets.text: The Department of Energy (DOE) lists the Strategic Petroleum Reserve's (SPR) maximum nominal drawdown capability at 4.4 million b/d with oil able to enter the market 13 days after a presidential decision, but effective capacity is lower: Big Hill's drawdown capability is currently zero because of a construction outage and West Hackberry is limited to 0.75 million b/d by low inventory.
bullets.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts); Wikipedia (citing DOE facility data)

bullets.text: From about 415 million barrels when the exchanges began in mid-March to 284.6 million in the week ending September 18, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) drew roughly 130 million barrels in about 27 weeks, an average pace of roughly 0.7 million b/d (Heavy Reading calculation from Department of Energy (DOE) and Energy Information Administration (EIA) figures).
bullets.source: Heavy Reading calculation (DOE via TS2.Tech; EIA via Energy Factbook)

bullets.text: The Senate-passed July 2025 budget bill cut Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) crude purchase funding to $171 million from the House's $1.3 billion, enough for roughly 3 million barrels instead of about 20 million at prevailing prices, according to Rapidan Energy cited in the reporting; the same bill kept the repeal of the last 7 million barrels of congressionally mandated SPR sales through fiscal year 2027 (Reuters).

gaps: DOE has not disclosed how many of the exchanged barrels have already been returned; the exact outstanding loan balance is not verifiable from a primary source.
The per-site (Bryan Mound, Big Hill, West Hackberry, Bayou Choctaw) inventory breakdown is published irregularly by DOE and was last seen weeks stale.
The composition (sweet vs sour) of the 2026 exchange deliveries is not published; matters for sour supply accounting.
Cushing stock level as a share of working capacity, the next binding constraint for WTI, is not available from the cited sources.

DOE has not published a borrower-by-borrower repayment ledger for the 2026 exchanges; Secretary Wright's September statement that returns begin early 2027 and run through 2029 at roughly 1.25 barrels per barrel borrowed is the only public schedule.
Final legislative status of the July 2025 repeal of the last 7-million-barrel congressionally mandated SPR sale (through FY2027) is unconfirmed from a primary legislative source.

Cushing working capacity (~75-76M bbl) and the ~20M-bbl operational-minimum threshold come from trade-press reporting, not EIA; the distance to the binding constraint for WTI is therefore an estimate.

watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the policy risk channel: Trump's energy posts move markets on sentiment first, and the archive below reconstructs what actually happened to differentials in past episodes so you can separate the noise from the move. Truth Social has no public API and blocks scrapers, so post text is quoted via media reporting, not direct post links. Each item carries its date.
watches.wcs_stakes: Trump is a first-order driver of the Canadian differential because tariff threats and energy policy talk reprice Western Canadian Select (WCS) treatment risk directly, as the 2025 episodes showed with the forward discount whipsawing between $12 and $16 per barrel. The 10% energy tariff rate, the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) exemptions, and the export ban being ruled out are the hard facts; the posts are the volatility around them. When tariff talk heats up, TMW is the instrument that prices it first.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, Trump is best read through the differential, not the headline: the archive shows WCS holding up remarkably well through the tariff episodes, with the real moves coming from policy facts rather than posts. Watch the USMCA annual-review cycle and any new tariff rounds for the next repricing; the export ban stays ruled out, which is the one policy that would have blown the differential out structurally. Treat the feed as sentiment and the archive as the base rate.

bullets.text: On Nov 25, 2024, President-elect Trump posted on Truth Social that on Jan 20 he would sign an executive order imposing a 25% tariff on ALL products from Canada and Mexico (plus an additional 10% on China), citing fentanyl and illegal border crossings. The post said the tariff would stay 'until such time as drugs, in particular Fentanyl, and all Illegal Aliens stop this Invasion of our country.'

The Nov 25, 2024 tariff threat moved FX immediately: the US dollar jumped over 2% against the Mexican peso and hit a four-year high against the Canadian dollar, as analysts warned the proposed tariffs would violate the USMCA Trump himself signed in 2020.

On Feb 1, 2025, Trump signed three IEEPA executive orders: 25% tariffs on all products of Canada and Mexico (effective Feb 4, 12:01 a.m. ET), with a lower 10% rate for Canadian 'energy products' (defined to include crude oil, natural gas, NGLs, refined products), and 10% on China. No exclusion process and no duty drawback were provided; a retaliation clause threatened higher duties if countries retaliated.

On Feb 3, 2025, Trump agreed to pause the Canada and Mexico tariffs for one month after calls with President Sheinbaum (Mexico agreed to send 10,000 National Guard troops to the border) and two calls with PM Trudeau (Canada committed new border-security resources). Trump confirmed the pause in Truth Social posts; Canada's planned retaliatory tariffs were also paused 30 days.

RBN Energy reported that the WCS forward discount was 'whipsawed in recent days as the threat of a 25% tariff on all exports from Canada by the newly minted Trump administration has waxed and waned'; as of Jan 10 the forward discount was ($12)/bbl to ($16)/bbl for Feb-Oct 2025 delivery months, 'a price range considered narrow by historical standards for this time of year.'

On Jan 21, 2025, discounts on heavy WCS for Q2 delivery widened to $13.75/bbl, up 50 cents on the day, after Trump said he planned to impose tariffs of as much as 25% on Canadian crude. The report noted prices had rallied the prior day 'on signs Trump wouldn't impose tariffs on Canadian crude,' showing the two-way whipsaw.

After the Feb 3 pause, WCS for March delivery narrowed to $13.50 under WTI on Feb 6, 2025, and Reuters reported that 'Canadian heavy crude prices have held up remarkably well' in the face of the tariff plan. TD Cowen said in a note: 'Investors believed a tariff announcement would immediately pressure the WCS heavy differential, but that has not proven to be the case,' with the discount 'not far off of what was seen prior to Trump's election.'

On March 4, 2025, the tariffs took effect (25% most Canadian goods, 10% energy products) and the WCS discount for April delivery widened to $13.70 under WTI, its widest since Feb 6. Energy analyst Rory Johnston said 'the threat of U.S. tariffs has been slowly creeping into the price of Canadian heavy crude over the last month' and warned that sustained tariffs 'will have a negative effect on investment appetite in the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin.' Canada exports roughly 4 million bpd of oil to the U.S., about 90% of its crude exports.

On March 6, 2025, Trump amended the tariff orders to exempt imports qualifying for duty-free treatment under the USMCA (effective March 7), announced via a Truth Social post after speaking with Mexico's Sheinbaum ('This Agreement is until April 2nd'). The same day Commerce Secretary Lutnick said the reprieve would 'likely cover all USMCA-compliant goods and services,' telling CNBC: 'if you lived under Donald Trump's US-Mexico-Canada agreement, you will get a reprieve from these tariffs now.'

On March 6, 2025, Bloomberg reported that Trump signed orders paring back the 25% IEEPA tariffs for USMCA-compliant goods until April 2, with Canadian potash facing a lower 10% duty. A White House official said some 62% of Canadian imports would be subject to the tariffs under historic data, 'with much of that energy products subject to a 10% rate.' Trump warned automakers he would not sign another extension: 'I told them that's it, this is a short-term deal.'

On April 2, 2025 ('Liberation Day'), Trump announced universal 10% and reciprocal tariffs on all trading partners, but Canada and Mexico did not appear on the reciprocal list because Trump had 'already levied a 25% tariff on all imports from the two nations excluding those items that fall under the USMCA'; the existing IEEPA tariffs on non-USMCA Canadian/Mexican goods remained in place.

On July 31, 2025, Trump signed an executive order increasing the tariff on Canadian goods from 25% to 35%, effective Aug 1, citing 'Canada's continued inaction and retaliation.' Energy and potash remained at the lower 10% rate per the CRS tariff-actions timeline (10% on energy imports effective March 4, 2025).

On Aug 22, 2025, PM Mark Carney announced Canada would drop many retaliatory tariffs to match the U.S. USMCA exemptions, saying 'Canada currently has the best trade deal with the United States.' Carney said over 85% of Canada-U.S. trade remained tariff-free and the U.S. average tariff rate on Canadian goods was 5.6%, the lowest among all U.S. trading partners. The decision followed a Thursday phone call in which Trump said, 'We are working on something. We want to be very good to Canada.'

On July 20-21, 2026, Trump announced 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods (energy products, potash, fish and critical minerals excluded), targeting Canada over alleged discrimination against U.S. autos, alcohol and dairy; the duty was to affect about $20 billion of U.S.-bound Canadian exports (~5% of shipments). Carney said he and Trump agreed to 'deepen and speed up' negotiations. The U.S. also opted against renewing USMCA for 16 years, subjecting the pact to annual reviews for a decade.

In April 2026, PM Carney said the scheduled USMCA review talks were turbulent: before formal negotiations began, the U.S. asked Canada for upfront concessions (changing or scrapping dairy supply management, provincial liquor bans, the Online Streaming Act and Online News Act). Carney listed Canada's own irritants: U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos and levies on forest products.
bullets.source: The Globe and Mail (via Ontario Legislative Library)

bullets.text: By end-March 2025, the Trump administration revoked the Biden-era general and specific oil licenses that had allowed Chevron and others to operate in Venezuela (companies had to wind up by May 27, 2025; Chevron kept only a limited 'essential operations' license). On March 24, 2025, Trump signed an executive order authorizing a 25% secondary tariff on any country importing Venezuelan oil directly or indirectly. Estimated impact: cutting Venezuelan output by 150,000-350,000 bpd.
bullets.source: American Journal of International Law (Cambridge Core)

bullets.text: Following Treasury's October 2025 designation of Russia's Lukoil and Rosneft, Chinese state-owned oil majors initially suspended Russian oil purchases, though Kpler data showed China kept buying significant volumes through smaller refiners. Chinese imports of Venezuelan oil also rose in 2025 after the U.S. revoked Chevron's general license, with Venezuela likely selling to China at a significant discount due to isolation.

On March 19, 2026, Trump officials told oil executives at an American Petroleum Institute board meeting that the administration had ruled out banning oil exports as a way to lower prices amid the escalating war with Iran. VP Vance, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum attended; Burgum told executives definitively that export restrictions were 'not under consideration.' WTI had crossed $101/bbl, up from $67 before the war began Feb 28, 2026.

HFI Research analysis of the export-ban rumor concluded it would be disastrous for the integrated system: U.S. shale would become landlocked, commercial crude storage would fill by May, producers would shut in output — and 'if US commercial crude storage builds too fast, it will jam up Canadian crude exports. WCS-WTI differentials will widen, Canadian crude inventories will fill up.'

On Jan 20, 2025, Trump declared a 'national energy emergency' and said in his inaugural address: 'We will drill, baby, drill.' The same day he signed executive orders reversing Biden-era orders restricting oil and gas exploration in Alaska, lifting restrictions on drilling in the Arctic Ocean, and seeking to open 625 million acres of offshore territory to drilling by reinstating rights revoked under Biden.

On Nov 20, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum signed the order 'Unleashing American Offshore Energy,' directing the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management to terminate Biden's 2024-2029 National OCS leasing program and develop an 11th program proposing up to 34 potential offshore lease sales across 21 areas off Alaska, 7 in the Gulf near Florida, and 6 off California.

On June 5, 2026, the Trump administration held a lease sale for 689,000 acres (60 tracts) in Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge — the first of four ANWR sales mandated by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The Biden administration received zero bids in its January 2025 ANWR sale of 400,000 acres, and the 2021 sale had few takers, despite USGS estimates of up to 11.8 billion barrels of technically recoverable oil.

On Jan 23, 2025, Trump told the World Economic Forum in Davos by video: 'I'm also going to ask Saudi Arabia and OPEC to bring down the cost of oil.' WTI futures slid 1.1% to settle below $75/bbl and Brent slipped near $78 on the remarks. He later tied lower prices to ending the Russia-Ukraine war: 'One way to stop it quickly is for OPEC to stop making so much money and drop the price of oil.'

In January 2025 Trump publicly threatened Russia with 'taxes, tariffs, and sanctions' if no Ukraine deal was struck, and Putin responded proposing a meeting on Ukraine and energy prices — positioning both sides for negotiations and adding oil-market volatility.

On Feb 24, 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social urging the company that was building Keystone XL to 'come back to America,' pledging 'easy approvals, almost immediate start' — 'The Trump Administration is very different (from the Biden administration) – Easy approvals, almost immediate start! If not them, perhaps another Pipeline Company. We want the Keystone XL Pipeline built.' Biden had revoked the permit in 2021; TC Energy spun its oil pipeline business into South Bow Energy.

On March 24, 2017, the Trump administration issued TransCanada a presidential permit for the Keystone XL pipeline, reversing Obama's rejection; the 1,179-mile line would have carried over 800,000 bpd of heavy crude from the Alberta oil sands to Nebraska, linking into networks feeding U.S. Gulf Coast refiners. It faced legal challenges and was halted after Biden revoked the permit in 2021.

On Oct 21, 2025, the Department of Energy issued a solicitation to buy 1 million barrels of crude for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at Bryan Mound, funded by $171 million appropriated in the Working Families Tax Cut. The SPR held just over 400 million barrels of ~700 million capacity after the 2022 drawdown of 180 million barrels; purchases were limited to U.S. companies with domestically sourced crude.

On Nov 12, 2025, DOE awarded the SPR contracts: ~1 million barrels from 18 offers by 6 companies, delivered to Bryan Mound Dec 1, 2025-Jan 31, 2026 — the first refill step under Trump's promise to restore the reserve to full operational capacity.

watches.title: The Global Sour Barrel
watches.dek: The sour grades WCS competes with, Dubai, Mars, Merey: how they are priced, and what moves the arb.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the comp sheet: Dubai, Mars, and Merey are the sour grades that price Western Canadian Select (WCS) by substitution, and the Brent-Dubai spread is the arb gauge between Atlantic and Asian sours. Reported differentials are point-in-time values, not a time series, and every bullet carries its vintage. No single public series tracks the full comp set, so compare like with like.
watches.wcs_stakes: The read right now is divergence: Western Canadian Select (WCS) printed an unusually wide $21 under West Texas Intermediate (WTI) on September 21 while the world sour comp set stayed mixed but firm — Saudi Aramco lifted November Arab Light to Asia to $4.00 over Oman/Dubai, and the Brent-Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS) hit $4.22 on September 27, its widest since July 8, even as Mars softened on freight costs and Asian spot buying stayed quiet. That says the wide Canadian print is more about Canadian barrels and logistics than a weak sour complex: US refineries are running at 97% with record diesel cracks bidding for heavy feedstock, and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) exchange barrels still flowing are the government's thumb on the sour scale until the 1.25x repayments start in 2027. This page is the cross-check on every TMW print: if the sour comp set holds firm and WCS goes wide, the differential is a buying opportunity, not a warning.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, this is the relative-value page: WCS against Mars, Dubai, and Merey tells you whether the differential is about Canadian barrels or the world sour barrel. Watch the Brent-Dubai spread, the Saudi and Iraqi official selling prices, and the SPR's sweet/sour draw mix as the marginal reads on sour supply. When the comp set firms together, the WCS differential usually follows.

sections.heading: Mars: the US Gulf sour benchmark

bullets.text: Mars crude, the Louisiana medium sour grade, weakened further against West Texas Intermediate (WTI) as rising shipping costs for US-to-Asia routes narrowed the export arb, per Bloomberg reporting on Sep 24. The move makes freight the deciding variable on whether US Gulf sours clear locally or sail to Asia.

Louisiana-delivered Mars settled at $87.65 per barrel in the March 2026 unwind, down about $20 per barrel from the prior session's Argus outright assessment, after comments from US President Donald Trump that the US-Israel war on Iran could end soon triggered a broad selloff. The volume-weighted average premium over West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell to $4.20 per barrel, about $8.50 per barrel lower than the prior session, with a high-to-low swing of about $10 per barrel. Mars also narrowed from a roughly $13.80 per barrel premium to June Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent futures to about $2.40 per barrel, and Southern Green Canyon traded as low as parity to Domestic Sweet (DSW) crude at Cushing, down from a $7.07 per barrel premium. The snap-back shows how much of the March premium was war risk rather than physical tightness.

sections.heading: Brent-Dubai EFS: the East-West sour arb gauge

bullets.text: S and P Global Platts data showed the November Brent/Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS) at 4.22 dollars a barrel on Sep 27, up 20 cents from the Sep 24 Asian close and its highest since July 8, when it was pegged at 4.29. Traders linked the climb to surging winter gas prices and expectations of gas-to-oil switching demand, while the October/November Dubai timespread held at a 1.03 dollar a barrel backwardation.

The same reporting noted September spot activity from Japan, India and China was minimal, keeping a lid on cash Dubai premiums despite the EFS strength. An unconfirmed Singapore trader report had October-loading Basrah Heavy sold to private Indian refiners at 50 to 70 cents a barrel below its Official Selling Price (OSP), a sign that physical sour premiums are not following paper.

The Brent-Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS), the spread between Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent futures and Dubai swaps, averaged $1.47 per barrel in the first half of January 2026, surged above $6 per barrel by March 3 as the Hormuz freeze took hold, averaged $9.12 per barrel in March, and oscillated between $3.05 and $16.25 per barrel through June and July. In stable conditions the EFS trades around $1.50 to $2.00 per barrel, and past spikes such as Abqaiq in 2019 and the Russia-Ukraine shock in 2022 barely nudged it above $1.50, making the 2026 move unprecedented in both scale and duration. In 2026 the geographic (routing security) component has overwhelmed the quality component, turning the EFS into a proxy for supply security rather than crude type, and it is the key East-West arb signal for Dubai-basket sour grades.

Saudi Aramco set its November 2026 official selling prices (OSPs) with Arab Light to East Asia at $4.00 per barrel over the Oman/Dubai average, up from $3.60 for October; to West Europe at $7.20 per barrel over (ICE) Brent, up from $5.70; to the Mediterranean at $6.30 per barrel over (ICE) Brent, up from $4.40; and to North America unchanged at $7.45 per barrel over the Argus Sour Crude Index (ASCI). Arab Medium and Arab Heavy to Asia were held flat at $3.45 and $1.70 over Oman/Dubai. The pattern, much bigger hikes for Europe than for Asia, prices in stronger European competition for sour barrels while testing how much Asian demand can absorb.
bullets.vintage: Announced early Sep 2026 for November 2026 loadings; accessed 2026-09-24
bullets.source: Argaam (November table; October comparison via Eye of Riyadh)

bullets.text: Basra Oil Company chief Bassem Abdul Karim said on Sep 24 that the northern leg now carries about 250,000 barrels per day of Basrah crude to Turkey's Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, while southern terminals handled about 2.6 million barrels per day. The same parliamentary hearing put Iraq's war-related revenue loss near 60 billion dollars and flagged sharply higher shipping costs.

Chatham House analysis published Sep 25 describes a proposed revival of the historic Kirkuk-Baniyas corridor, routed via a new hub at Haditha, that would give Baghdad a 2-million-barrel-per-day Hormuz bypass at an estimated cost near 15 billion dollars and roughly four years of construction, reportedly backed by the Trump administration. The piece cautions it diversifies rather than replaces Hormuz, since most Iraqi barrels are bound for China and India, which sit closer to the Gulf than to the Mediterranean.

The Syrian Petroleum Company's Refining Directorate said the first consignment of about 32,800 metric tons of gasoline arrived by tanker at Baniyas and is moving to the Iraqi border by truck under a transit contract with Qatar's UCC Holding, which supplies the fuel and manages transport. Iraq's Oil Ministry confirmed the arrangement; the deal is gasoline-only for now but the route could later carry crude.
bullets.vintage: Week of Sep 21-26, 2026; published Sep 26, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28
bullets.source: Freedom Bunker (via The Cradle and Reuters)

bullets.text: Iraq's crude exports jumped 73 percent in August 2026 to 73 million barrels for the month (about 2.34 million barrels per day), the highest level since the Iran war began, after the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) sold Basrah crude at discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel to offset extreme shipping and insurance costs and a small number of Iraqi tankers received special Iranian permission to transit the Strait of Hormuz. The rebound returned more than $4.5 billion of medium-sour crude to the market in a single month, directly relieving the Dubai-basket sour shortfall that had supported Mars and other Atlantic Basin sours.

Iraq's State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy for collection by ship-to-ship (STS) transfer near the Omani coast for September delivery via tender, the first time since the Iran war began that buyers could lift Iraqi crude outside the Persian Gulf instead of loading deep inside it. Vitol Group and TotalEnergies were among the largest traders moving Iraqi oil during the war, and SOMO also tendered fuel oil for pickup inside or outside the Gulf. If the outside-Hormuz loading point becomes routine, it structurally lowers the freight risk embedded in Basrah pricing and narrows the crisis premium in Dubai-linked grades.

The US government's own sour barrel is shifting grade: DOE's August 20 grade table showed the SPR at 101.8 million barrels sweet and 192.3 million sour, and by September 11 the split was 96.8 million sweet and 188.1 million sour (Reuters), meaning sweet drew about 5.0 million barrels against 4.2 million of sour over roughly three weeks. With the reserve at roughly 34% sweet versus DOE's 40% design target, the government's remaining emergency supply is getting more sour-dominant, which limits how much sweet relief a future release could actually deliver to light-sweet markets.
bullets.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts); Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine)

bullets.text: The seven core producers of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC+) and its allies (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman) met virtually on September 6, 2026 and held October production quotas at September levels, the first month since April without an increase. The decision follows the August 2 approval of a 188,000 barrel per day September increase (Saudi Arabia and Russia 62,000 each, Iraq 26,000, Kuwait 16,000, Kazakhstan 10,000, Algeria 6,000, Oman 5,000), which completed the unwinding of the 2023 voluntary cuts. October required levels: Saudi Arabia 10.478 million barrels per day, Russia 9.949, Iraq 4.431, Kuwait 2.676, Kazakhstan 1.628, Algeria 1.007, Oman 0.841. Delegates expect quotas to hold through year-end while a 2027 baseline review runs; the next review is October 4.
bullets.source: NewsGoLive (quoting OPEC statement); September increase detail via World Oil

bullets.text: A record 3.5 million barrels per day of US crude was scheduled to arrive in Asia-Pacific for June 2026 delivery, with Japan alone taking more than 530,000 barrels per day versus a prior monthly high of 290,000 in December 2025, as Asian complex refiners substituted Dubai-basket sour grades with Atlantic Basin barrels. India's July arrivals included 2.8 million barrels per day of Russian Urals (over 55 percent of imports), while Reliance's Jamnagar complex took record volumes of Latin American, US and Canadian barrels and blended them to approximate a medium-sour feedstock. The flow shows Asian sour demand leaking out of the Dubai pricing system entirely, which caps how much support the sour complex can draw from Asian buying.
bullets.source: Petroleum Economist (citing S&P Global Commodity Insights)

sections.heading: Refining economics: max runs, deferred cokers, record diesel cracks

bullets.text: US refineries ran at 97 percent utilization in the week ending Sep 11, with no idle capacity left to switch on. US distillate production averaged 5.1 million barrels per day from January through August, the most since 2019, while distillate inventories sat 15.8 million barrels, or 13 percent, below the five-year seasonal average. The read for sour crude: heavy sour barrels with high distillate yields stay bid as long as this lasts.
bullets.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 11, 2026; published Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: US refinery utilization hit 97.4 percent in late August 2026, the highest since 2018, and shipbroker Gibson reports very little autumn maintenance is confirmed because robust margins keep refiners from taking units offline. The only confirmed turnaround on the Petroleum Administration for Defense District 3 (PADD 3) slate is ExxonMobil's Beaumont fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) unit plus at least two hydrotreaters, running about 45 days from early December to mid-January. PBF pushed Chalmette's crude distillation unit (CDU) and coker into 2027 and CITGO did the same with the Lake Charles coker, while Valero guided third-quarter Gulf Coast throughput at 1.78 to 1.83 million barrels per day. The International Energy Agency (IEA) still expects October North America runs of 18.8 million barrels per day versus 20.5 in August. Sustained near-max runs keep US Gulf Coast (USGC) coker demand for Mars, Western Canadian Select (WCS) and Merey-type barrels elevated, but deferred maintenance raises unplanned-outage risk.

Asian refining margins for 10 parts per million (ppm) sulfur diesel surged to a record just above $87 per barrel in mid-September 2026, versus pre-war levels around $22 per barrel and a prior record of $85.60 set in late March 2026, while the front-month diesel spread stood slightly above $11 per barrel, near a five-month high. Because medium-sour grades carry higher distillate yields than light sweets, record diesel cracks directly support bids for Mars-type barrels and widen the incentive for complex refiners to run heavy sour slates.

sections.heading: Mexican Maya: the disappearing USGC heavy barrel

bullets.text: Pemex crude exports fell to a 35-year low of about 368,000 barrels per day in December 2025, down 54 percent year over year, as the Olmeca refinery (Dos Bocas) ramped to over 260,000 barrels per day of heavy crude processing and absorbed barrels once destined for export. The export collapse removed roughly 440,000 barrels per day of heavy sour supply year over year, and US imports from Mexico fell to 224,500 barrels per day in December (down 22 percent month over month). With crude production capped at 1.8 million barrels per day under Mexico's Energy Sovereignty 2030 roadmap, the industry may lean more heavily on Western Canadian Select (WCS) or Mars as the Americas heavy benchmark as Maya liquidity dries up.

The Maya export collapse partially reversed as Pemex's refineries stumbled: the Olmeca (Dos Bocas) refinery, with 340,000 barrels per day of nameplate capacity, averaged only 144,000 barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026 (about 42 percent utilization) after a January electrical failure knocked out its coker, catalytic and hydrodesulfurization units, deferring around 150,000 barrels of crude processing. Mexican crude exports averaged about 550,000 barrels per day in March through May 2026, down from roughly 780,000 a year earlier, while fuel imports climbed to 700,000 barrels per day in June. If domestic plants keep underperforming, Maya barrels could swing back onto the US Gulf Coast (USGC) export market, so the heavy-sour shortfall is not one-directional.

sections.heading: WCS against the sour comp set

bullets.text: The Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) stood at 21 dollars a barrel on Sep 21, per Argus market reporting, an unusually wide differential for 2026. With Friday's WTI settlement at 92.44 dollars, implied WCS was 71.44 dollars a barrel, down about 7.09 dollars on the week as the Brent-WTI spread hit 11.93 dollars, its widest of 2026. Goldman Sachs' fourth-quarter 2026 Brent target of 85 dollars a barrel translates to WCS near 59 dollars, roughly 12.44 dollars below the current implied level.
bullets.source: Oil Authority (citing Argus and Goldman Sachs)

bullets.text: An infographic from Modern Miracle Network, citing Bloomberg and Argus data, says zero percent of Vancouver-to-Asia crude used the Southern California ship-to-ship transfer to very large crude carriers in August 2026, versus 78 percent in June 2024, with direct Aframax shipments across the Pacific costing about 54 percent of the California-transfer route. Treat as an unconfirmed lead: the economics are plausible given elevated very large crude carrier rates, but it comes from an advocacy account, not a newsroom.

Western Canadian Select (WCS) at Hardisty, Alberta traded at an $8.50 per barrel discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) on June 2, 2026, tightening from $9.75 on May 26, as wildfires shut in nearly 350,000 barrels per day of Canadian output (Cenovus's Christina Lake alone lost about 238,000 barrels per day). S&P Global Commodity Insights analysts noted that lower volumes from Mexico and Venezuela to the US Gulf Coast (USGC) have also limited heavy sour supply, and that Chevron's exit from Venezuela was expected to pull up to 200,000 barrels per day of heavy crude from the USGC. The episode shows WCS pricing off the same shrinking USGC heavy-sour pool that Mars and Merey serve.

gaps: No public price history series for Dubai, Mars, Merey or WCS was found in open sources; differentials cited are point-in-time reported values, not a time series.
Current (September 2026) assessed values for Mars and Dubai premiums/discounts are behind paywalls (S&P Global Platts, Argus).
The exact composition of the SPR's 2026 exchange deliveries (sweet vs sour split) is not published.
No public source for current WCS forward-month differential values beyond reported broker quotes.

No public time series exists for the Brent-Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS); the 2026 crisis arc (sub-$2 to over $15 per barrel) is stitched from point-in-time figures in the Petroleum Economist, not a continuous series.

Iraqi SOMO November 2026 official selling prices for Basrah grades could not be corroborated: a real-time wire reported Basrah Medium to Asia at plus $0.85 per barrel to Oman/Dubai while an Argus sample table showed plus $2.10, so no Iraqi OSP bullet was drafted.

No public monthly series confirms whether Mexico's crude export collapse (368,000 barrels per day in December 2025) persisted through 2026; the March-May 2026 average of about 550,000 barrels per day comes from a single OilPrice analysis, not Pemex data.

watches.title: OPEC and Middle East Supply Watch
watches.dek: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies (OPEC+) quotas, the Middle East supply disruption, Gulf loadings, and Saudi pricing: the state of the world's swing supply.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the supply-side bid for sour barrels: OPEC+ quota decisions set the ceiling, the Middle East conflict sets the actual flow, and Saudi official selling prices set the price signal Asian buyers see. Each bullet carries its vintage, so read 2026 wartime data against the pre-war baselines in the Hormuz watch. The disagreements log flags where trackers and officials genuinely diverge.
watches.wcs_stakes: The Gulf tap is open: Saudi crude exports averaged 5.28 million b/d over September 1-23, the strongest pace since the conflict began, and OPEC+ held October quotas flat -- the first month without an increase since April -- with compliance near 115%. That is the fundamental headwind on every sour premium Western Canadian Select (WCS) competes against: the more Gulf medium and heavy sour that loads, the less refiners need to chase substitute barrels. The forward risk is asymmetric: if Hormuz flows normalize or the 2027 baseline review unlocks more OPEC+ barrels, the sour premium collapses and Canadian differentials lose their relative bid; a fresh disruption does the opposite.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, this page is the fundamental backdrop behind every TMW and ARV print: tight Gulf sour supply is what is keeping the heavy basis bid right now. If Hormuz flows normalize or Saudi pricing turns aggressive again, expect the Canadian differential complex, including TMW and ARV, to soften first at the margin.

sections.heading: The pause: quotas held after the unwind

bullets.text: The seven OPEC+ producers that unwound the 2023 voluntary cuts will meet again on October 4, 2026 to set November production levels, keeping the monthly review cadence in place. Independent capacity assessments are due by the end of September, and their results are meant to set the reference production levels that will anchor 2027 quotas. Full ministerial talks on December output policy are expected on November 4, according to OPEC statements.
bullets.vintage: OPEC announcement Sep 7, 2026; published Sep 10, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: OPEC+ compliance averaged about 115 percent in September against 119 percent in August, according to a delegate cited by Argus. The figures remain preliminary until confirmed by the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC), the group's technical body. High compliance in wartime means the restraint is real, but it also means the group has less short-term room to offset further Gulf disruptions.
bullets.vintage: Event: Sep 2026; published Sep 24, 2026 (single delegate source, preliminary); accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: OPEC+ approved a 188,000 barrel-per-day production increase for September 2026 and then agreed to hold required production levels flat for October, the first pause since the unwind began in April; required levels include Saudi Arabia at 10.478 million barrels per day, Russia at 9.949 million, Iraq at 4.431 million, Kuwait at 2.676 million, Kazakhstan at 1.628 million, Algeria at 1.007 million, and Oman at 0.841 million, with the next meeting scheduled for October 4.

Reuters sources said on July 28, 2026 that OPEC+ was likely to keep production increases on hold after September, noting that most of the announced hikes existed only on paper because the Iran war forced Middle East export cuts, and that the group was not expected to change policy until year-end, with 2027 quotas to be set after a capacity review.

sections.heading: The war's mark on Gulf output

bullets.text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sep 25 that Tehran had conveyed a seven-day plan to Washington through Qatari mediators at the United Nations General Assembly: if the US lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waived oil sanctions, released frozen Iranian assets and observed a ceasefire covering the region including Lebanon, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks within seven days. President Trump publicly rejected the proposal on Sep 26, calling it not acceptable; the Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects US strikes could resume after November's midterm elections.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Sep 24 that France will send soldiers, radar systems and defense systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, a key node for Saudi energy exports that has come under Houthi missile attacks. Macron said the deployment was agreed with Riyadh and framed as defensive, not as French involvement in the wider conflict. Saudi Arabia said on Sep 24 its air defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles launched toward the Yanbu and Taif areas.

The US Maritime Administration urged US-flagged commercial vessels to switch off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders when transiting high-risk waters around the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, under guidance effective Sep 23, and to vary routes and limit electronic transmissions. The advisory follows a resumption of Houthi attacks on commercial shipping, including missile strikes on two tankers off Yanbu in August, and a Houthi-declared ban on Saudi maritime navigation through the Bab el-Mandeb strait announced July 20.
bullets.vintage: Guidance effective Sep 23, 2026; published Sep 25, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: OPEC's September Monthly Oil Market Report showed OPEC 12 crude output rising 346,000 barrels per day from July to August, driven by a 664,000 barrel-per-day jump in Iraq that more than offset declines of 399,000 in Iran and 75,000 in Saudi Arabia. OPEC put group spare capacity at 5.066 million barrels per day, with the Big 4's sustained capacity at 21.449 million, reflecting a 600,000 barrel-per-day capacity gain in the United Arab Emirates since 2022. The report also expects US tight oil to grow by only 50,000 barrels per day in 2026 and stay flat in 2027, far below the EIA's projections.
bullets.source: Seeking Alpha (citing OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report)

bullets.text: OPEC's July 2026 Monthly Oil Market Report showed June secondary-source output of 22.002 million barrels per day, up 3.051 million month on month, but the composition reflects the war: Saudi Arabia produced 6.847 million barrels per day (down 99,000), Iraq 1.970 million (up 446,000), Kuwait 1.452 million (up 880,000), Iran 2.441 million (up 155,000), and the United Arab Emirates 3.809 million (up 1.642 million).
bullets.source: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) Monthly Oil Market Report

bullets.text: The EIA's September 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook estimated that 6.7 million barrels per day of Middle East crude production was shut in during August, up from 5.0 million in July, easing to about 5.7 million in the fourth quarter, with regional output staying below pre-conflict averages until the second quarter of 2027.
bullets.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA) Short-Term Energy Outlook, via Oil and Gas Journal summary

bullets.text: The EIA estimated that the conflict has removed about 400 million barrels from global oil inventories since the start of the year, and forecast Brent crude near $90 per barrel in the second half of 2026 amid the Middle East disruptions.
bullets.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA) Short-Term Energy Outlook, via Oil and Gas Journal summary

bullets.text: Saudi Arabia's crude exports averaged 5.28 million barrels per day over September 1-23, the strongest pace since the conflict began, with about 3.4 million barrels per day loading at Gulf ports, according to Bloomberg ship-tracking data. Analyst Rory Johnston of Commodity Context wrote on Sep 26 that Hormuz oil flows had reached roughly 13.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average, about two-thirds of prewar levels, citing Kpler data. Kpler separately put total September Middle East oil exports at 12.8 million barrels per day, the highest since the war began in February but still more than 6 million below prewar.

Iraq's Ministry of Oil clarified on Sep 22 that September crude exports are averaging about 2.6 million barrels per day, correcting media reports of 4 million barrels per day that reflected a single day's spike including a State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) shipment routed outside the strait. Exports had topped 3 million barrels per day in the first week of September, the highest since the conflict began, but Reuters reported a more than 400,000 barrel-per-day slide over the month. The ministry described the rate as a significant achievement given the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
bullets.source: Iraq Business News (citing the Ministry of Oil)

bullets.text: Vitol bought at least 25 million barrels of deeply discounted Iraqi crude in September, becoming Iraq's second-largest crude buyer behind the United Arab Emirates' ADNOC at 40 million barrels, two sources told Reuters. Bloomberg reported on Sep 26 that SOMO is now offering last-minute cargoes as traders back out, with sky-high freight adding about 20 dollars a barrel on the Gulf of Oman to East Asia route and SOMO cutting prices on Basrah Medium and Heavy grades in recent tenders.

Kpler data cited September 23, 2026 showed about 6.5 million barrels per day flowing through the Strait of Hormuz so far in September, the highest since the June ceasefire but down from roughly 20 million barrels per day before the conflict; very large crude carrier (VLCC) freight from the Middle East Gulf to China hit an all-time high of about $30 per barrel, roughly 25 percent of cargo cost.

A September 10-11, 2026 drone attack shut Saudi Arabia's East-West (Petroline) pipeline, a 1,200-kilometer line with about 7 million barrels per day of capacity; Kpler estimated storage at Yanbu below 15 million barrels, and Aramco cancelled or delayed some September cargoes to European refiners.

Three sources told Reuters on September 23, 2026 that Saudi Arabia resumed pumping through the East-West pipeline on September 22 after the drone attacks; Iraq is exporting more than 3 million barrels per day and targeting over 600,000 barrels per day through the Turkey pipeline, while preliminary August estimates of total Iraqi exports differed between trackers: Vortexa at 2.3 million barrels per day and Kpler at 2.17 million, versus pre-war figures of 3.7 million and 3.362 million respectively.

Kpler data cited September 22, 2026 put Asia's crude imports at 23.96 million barrels per day in September, the highest since February and up from 23.38 million in August, though still 13 percent below pre-conflict levels; US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on September 21 that as much as 15 million barrels per day was still leaving the Middle East, while tanker-tracking services put observed exports lower.

sections.heading: Saudi pricing: the sour barrel signal

bullets.text: Aramco cut its July 2026 Arab Light official selling price (OSP) for Asia by $11 per barrel to $1.50 below the Oman/Dubai benchmark, the largest single-month reduction in more than two decades; traders said Asian buyers, already satisfied with their crude slate, were unlikely to be swayed, with renewed Iranian competition for Asian buyers cited as a factor in the cut.

OPEC's September 2026 Monthly Oil Market Report cut its 2026 oil demand growth forecast for the fifth straight month, lowering it by 200,000 barrels per day to 380,000, with total consumption at 105.84 million barrels per day; it raised the 2027 growth forecast to 2.36 million barrels per day and noted July OPEC+ output of 38.055 million barrels per day.

The United Arab Emirates withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+ effective May 1, 2026, according to the September report, which also cut cumulative 2026 demand growth by about 1 million barrels per day since the US-Iran war began.

gaps: Exact per-country September compliance versus required levels was not yet published at the time of writing.
Day-to-day Hormuz barrel flows are tracker estimates; the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) quarterly volume series lags by months.
The 2027 quota framework depends on an OPEC+ capacity review not yet completed.

watches.title: Condensate and diluent watch
watches.dek: The other half of every Western Canadian Select (WCS) barrel: what diluent is, where Alberta's condensate comes from, the structural import shortfall, and the cost it puts on the heavy barrel.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the cost line inside every Western Canadian Select (WCS) barrel. Trade press usually means pentanes plus (C5+) when it says condensate, the Alberta Energy Regulator's (AER) formal category. Every bullet carries its vintage: 2026 trade-press snapshots sit against the AER's annual ST98 supply and demand balance, the benchmark source.
watches.wcs_stakes: The so-what on diluent is cost, not price: roughly 30% of every dilbit barrel is condensate priced near West Texas Intermediate (WTI), and Alberta is structurally short -- 2024 pentanes-plus production of 396,000 b/d against 751,000 b/d of demand, with the two US import lines (Cochin at about 95,000 b/d, Southern Lights at about 195,000 b/d) running at or near full. When diluent tightens, the cost hits bitumen netbacks directly even if the TMW print does not move. Fresh signal: FTAI Energy Partners agreed on September 28 to buy the Port Arthur crude terminal and half of the Hardisty Diluent Recovery Unit, midstream money betting that diluent recovery and Gulf Coast placement stay economic.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, watch the AER's ST98 supply and demand balance and the utilization of the two condensate import lines as the leading indicators. If imports saturate and the spot condensate premium firms, bitumen netbacks shrink from the cost side while the TMW print may not move at all. Cheap diluent is as important to the WCS barrel as strong refinery demand.

sections.heading: What diluent is, and why bitumen needs it

bullets.text: Dilbit is bitumen diluted with natural gas condensate, typically 30 to 35% by volume. It accounts for about 60% of all marketable crude production from the oil sands, and with the exception of the Kearl and Fort Hills mines, all of it comes from thermal in situ facilities.

Bitumen is extra heavy and almost solid at room temperature. Undiluted bitumen is non-marketable because it cannot be stored or shipped by pipeline, so it must be upgraded or diluted with a lighter hydrocarbon.

Alberta pipeline specifications require crude under 350 centistokes of viscosity and density under 940 kilograms per cubic metre (above 18.9 American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity). Condensate at 30% by volume or more is added to bitumen to meet that spec, producing dilbit.

Imperial Oil's investor materials define WCS, the Canadian heavy benchmark, as about one-quarter diluent and three-quarters bitumen, and the bitumen realization bridge backs the diluent cost out of the WCS price. Diluent is not a footnote, it is a line item in the netback.
bullets.source: Imperial Oil investor presentation (via US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing)

sections.heading: The balance: Alberta is structurally short

bullets.text: In 2024, Alberta pentanes plus production averaged 396.2 thousand barrels per day, up 6.8% year on year on higher recovery at field plants. Alberta demand reached 751.1 thousand barrels per day, up 5.1%, driven by higher bitumen production. The province consumed nearly twice what it produced.
bullets.source: Alberta Energy Regulator, ST98 2025 (Alberta Energy Outlook)

bullets.text: The AER's base-case forecast has pentanes plus production growing to 471.5 thousand barrels per day by 2034 while demand reaches 933.7 thousand barrels per day. Imports of pentanes plus into Alberta are expected to increase over the forecast period to cover the widening shortfall.
bullets.source: Alberta Energy Regulator, ST98 2025 (Alberta Energy Outlook)

bullets.text: The Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin (WCSB) imports roughly 260,000 barrels per day of condensate from the US to meet demand. Canada produces about 570,000 barrels per day of condensate, primarily from Montney and Duvernay unconventional plays, with the balance imported by pipeline.
Almost all of Western Canada's refined petroleum product imports from the US are condensate, which is used to blend with heavy bitumen so the blended bitumen can move by pipeline.
bullets.source: Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (CAPP), Canadian Refining Industry deck

sections.heading: Pricing: condensate trades near or above WTI

bullets.text: Condensate is a premium light stream: Oil Sands Magazine notes that condensate and synthetic crude produced through bitumen upgrading can trade close to par or even at a small premium to West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the US benchmark.

Enverus Intelligence Research expects condensate prices to stay robust as oil sands growth lifts in-basin demand, a tailwind for producers with exposure to the liquids-rich Montney and Duvernay and for select midstreamers.

The arithmetic is unforgiving: every dilbit barrel carries about 30% condensate priced near WTI while the blended barrel sells at a heavy discount to WTI. When the condensate premium firms, bitumen producers absorb the cost, not refiners.
bullets.source: Oil Sands Magazine (differentials page); Imperial Oil realization bridge (SEC filing)

bullets.text: FTAI Energy Partners, the midstream arm of FTAI Infrastructure, has agreed to buy the Port Arthur crude terminal in Texas and a 50 percent stake in the Diluent Recovery Unit (DRU) at Hardisty, Alberta, from USD Group. Diluent Recovery Units strip diluent from diluted bitumen so the condensate can be recycled back into Alberta's diluent pool rather than being exported with the barrel, which reduces the basin's structural reliance on imported diluent. The cash consideration is about 255 million US dollars, with closing expected in the fourth quarter of 2026 pending regulatory approvals; the release does not disclose the DRU's throughput capacity.

Two pipelines carry US condensate into the WCSB: Pembina's Cochin at about 95,000 barrels per day and Enbridge's Southern Lights at about 195,000 barrels per day. Both have been running at or near full capacity.
Enbridge is planning a 15,000 barrel-per-day expansion of Southern Lights to ship additional diluent to heavy oil producers, part of its broader Mainline and regional system optimization program.

Diluent recovery units (DRUs) would recycle diluent at Edmonton rail terminals instead of importing it. Cenovus studied a unit to process 180,000 barrels per day of dilbit and recover 60,000 barrels per day of diluent for return to northern Alberta projects, at an estimated cost of $800 million to $1 billion. Imperial Oil ruled a DRU out for now, citing high cost and market uncertainty.

Eight Capital's analysis at the time estimated that DRUs at rail-loading terminals could free about one-third of each railcar's space and add roughly 190,000 barrels per day of incremental bitumen capacity if applied across 600,000 barrels per day of crude-by-rail. No major DRU has been built since.

Enverus estimates non-upgraded Canadian oil sands production rises by about 100,000 barrels per day per year through 2028, which drives in-basin condensate demand higher each year. The highest-yielding condensate regions of the Montney in BC and Alberta cannot grow fast enough, so a supply gap becomes apparent within a couple of years.

There is a trade-off: the condensate-directed drilling that feeds the diluent pool also produces associated natural gas, which puts downward pressure on Alberta Energy Company (AECO) gas hub prices. Robust condensate demand is good for liquids-rich producers and bad for dry-gas producers.

Monthly tracking: the AER publishes in situ oil sands production volumes in ST53 and broader oil sands production, supply, and disposition in ST39, both monthly. The annual ST98 outlook is where the condensate supply and demand balance is formally reconciled.
bullets.source: Alberta Energy Regulator (ST53 and ST39 statistical reports)

gaps: There is no monthly public series for Alberta condensate production outside the annual ST98 outlook, so the real-time balance is opaque between editions.
Enbridge and Pembina do not publish continuous utilization on Southern Lights and Cochin, so 'near capacity' claims are snapshot estimates.
Owner-level diluent buying, spot versus term, and storage levels are private; this page tracks only the aggregate balance.

watches.title: Refinery margins watch
watches.dek: Crack spreads, utilization, and turnarounds: how refinery economics set the bid for discounted heavy barrels like Western Canadian Select (WCS).
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the demand-side bid under the heavy barrel. The 3-2-1 crack spread is the industry's shorthand for refinery profitability, utilization shows how hard plants are running, and the turnaround calendar shows when crude demand dips. Every bullet carries its vintage. Regional benchmarks differ, so compare like with like.
watches.wcs_stakes: Margins say run, but WCS went wide anyway: the 3-2-1 crack stood at $73.12 a barrel on September 22, near the May 2022 record, yet the Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount printed an unusually wide $21 under West Texas Intermediate (WTI) on September 21. The 3-2-1 is not grade-specific: it prices a light barrel through a generic refinery, while WCS is priced by coker economics -- which heavy barrel wins the marginal coker slot. A record crack with a wide WCS print is consistent with constrained coking capacity choosing between competing heavies, not weak demand -- though public weekly data do not directly observe coker availability, so saturation stays an inference. The mechanism: pipes running near full (October apportionment was announced at 8 percent for lights and 4 percent for heavies) push the marginal barrel down to the US Gulf Coast, where coking capacity looks constrained and Venezuelan exports, now moving under US control and marketed by Vitol and Trafigura, are offered at steep discounts for the same runs (the traders seeking Brent minus $18-20 for Merey). The Joliet outage (ExxonMobil's 275,000 b/d plant, shut September 13, restarting September 23) punched a local hole in PADD 2 (the Petroleum Administration for Defense Districts covering the Midwest) demand, but the plant is back in service, so that leg is fading. The forward risk: when cracks compress and the fall turnaround slate hits, discounted heavy barrels strand first and the differential widens for real.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, this page is the demand-side complement to the supply watches: watch PADD 2 utilization and the fall turnaround slate the way you watch TMW. While cracks sit near record highs, refineries have every incentive to run hard and bid for discounted heavy barrels, which supports WCS. The risk is the turn: when maintenance or margin compression takes runs down, heavy barrels lose their bid first.

bullets.text: A crack spread measures the difference between the purchase price of crude oil and the selling price of finished products, such as gasoline and distillate fuel, that a refinery produces from the crude. It is an indicator of the short-term profit margin of refineries, but it excludes other variable costs and all fixed costs.
bullets.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

bullets.text: The 3-2-1 spread approximates the product yield at a typical US refinery: for every three barrels of crude oil processed, the refinery makes two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillate fuel.
bullets.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

bullets.text: The calculation: add the spot price for two barrels of gasoline to one barrel of diesel (multiplying per-gallon quotes by 42 gallons per barrel), subtract the price of three barrels of crude, and divide by three to get a spread in dollars per barrel.
bullets.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

bullets.text: The 3-2-1 crack spread is the most widely used benchmark for US refiner profitability. It is traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), where refiners use it as a hedging instrument to lock in their margins.

The Trading Economics Crack Spread index, which tracks the spread between crude oil and refined products at the average US refinery, surged to a record 75 dollars a barrel in September 2026, up nearly 200 percent since mid-February. The report ties the spike to disrupted Middle East crude exports that pushed US refiners to run above 100 percent of nameplate capacity, and says the presidential administration weighed a ban on diesel exports as domestic gasoline and diesel prices climbed.

The 3-2-1 crack spread stood at 73.12 dollars a barrel on Sep 22, about 3.7 percent below the May 13, 2022 record of 75.89 and far above the post-2006 median near 19 dollars. The benchmark is a gross spot margin before operating costs, Renewable Identification Number (RIN) costs, transport, and refinery-specific yields, and refiners' reported margins lag it by roughly a quarter. RBN Energy's daily print had the spread at 68.19 dollars on Sep 27, showing it cooling off the record but still near triple the median.
bullets.source: thetrading.tools (computed from EIA daily spot prices)

bullets.text: US gasoline futures held above 3.45 dollars a gallon on Sep 23, the highest since May 21, as the crack spread hit record highs and refiners shifted output toward higher-priced diesel ahead of winter, tightening gasoline supply. The note also cites continued Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refining and reports that Russia is set to extend its diesel export ban beyond September.

On July 17, 2026, the 3-2-1 crack spread closed at $69.66 per barrel, a record high for the third consecutive session. Diesel, the biggest portion of global oil consumption, was the primary driver. US diesel stockpiles were just over 102 million barrels, nearly 11 million below the February 27 level and about 8 million below the five-year seasonal average, per US Energy Information Administration (EIA) data.

The West Texas Intermediate (WTI) 3-2-1 crack spread hit $59 per barrel in August 2026, nearly triple its January level and the highest since the 2020 pandemic crash. The 2010 to 2021 average was about $19 per barrel. The six-month forward curve was pricing about $44, still 35% above the long-run average.

The diesel crack crossed $100 per barrel in August. Gasoline refining margins were $45 to $50 per barrel and jet kerosene $70 to $75, per BloombergNEF data. Diesel effectively left its historical range.

By September 24, the gasoline-over-crude margin had widened to about $58 per barrel, more than triple the 20-year median of $17 and in the 99.8th percentile of every trading day since 2006. US refinery utilization hit 97.4% in late August, the highest since 2018.

The spike's drivers: the Iran war disrupted Middle East product exports, Russia restricted diesel exports, Ukrainian drone strikes hit 21 of Russia's 38 large refineries, and US refiners became the supplier of last resort, pushing fuel exports to record highs while domestic stockpiles drained.
bullets.source: Reuters (via BOE Report); Real Investment Advice

sections.heading: PADD 2: the Midwest runs flat out

bullets.text: ExxonMobil entered Friday, September 18 with its 275,000 barrel-per-day Joliet, Illinois refinery still shut, roughly a week after the September 13 power outage and a subsequent flood that overwhelmed a pump, with no firm restart timetable given. The plant produces about 11 million gallons of gasoline and diesel per day and accounts for roughly 6 percent of Midwest refining capacity, making each extra offline day a material hole in regional supply.

Several units at ExxonMobil's Joliet refinery returned to service on Wednesday, Sep 23, starting the restart of the full plant after the September 13 site-wide shutdown, and the refinery was reported back in service around Sep 27. Detail sits behind a paywall; the restart arc is confirmed by the publisher's own headlines and the public restart sequence.

In August, US refinery utilization was 97.4% nationally and 101.8% in the Midwest (PADD 2, the Petroleum Administration for Defense District covering the Midwest), per EIA and BloombergNEF data. Readings above 100% reflect the EIA measuring gross input against nominal operable capacity, with debottlenecking pushing actual throughput above it.
bullets.source: Seven Gates Research (citing EIA and BloombergNEF)

bullets.text: For the week ending September 18, 2026, US refiners processed less crude, and it was not seasonal maintenance: Exxon's Joliet refinery had been mostly offline since the prior Sunday after a power outage, with floodwater also an issue. The plant accounts for 6 to 8% of regional refining capacity, and the PADD 2 utilization drop pressured an already tight Midwest product market.
bullets.source: Tim Dallinger (EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report summary)

bullets.text: That same week, US gasoline inventories were about 6% below the five-year seasonal average and distillate about 12% below. Simple cracks moved back toward record high rates.
bullets.source: Tim Dallinger (EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report summary)

bullets.text: Marathon Petroleum's Q2 2026 refining margin more than doubled to $36.33 per barrel from $17.58 a year earlier, on higher crack spreads across all operating regions. Its refineries ran at 94% of capacity with 2.9 million barrels per day of throughput. The Mid-Continent regional margin was $33.68 per barrel.

The Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) stood at 21 dollars a barrel on Sep 21, per Argus market reporting, an unusually wide differential for 2026. With Friday's WTI settlement at 92.44 dollars, implied WCS was 71.44 dollars a barrel, down about 7.09 dollars on the week. Goldman Sachs' fourth-quarter 2026 Brent target of 85 dollars a barrel translates to WCS near 59 dollars, roughly 12.44 dollars below the current implied level.
bullets.source: Oil Authority (citing Argus and Goldman Sachs)

bullets.text: Midwest refiners invested billions of dollars in coking units to turn Canadian heavy crude into gasoline and diesel. BP's 430,000 barrel-per-day Whiting, Indiana refinery can process up to 85% heavy crude, up from 20% before the upgrades. That conversion hardware is the structural bid under WCS.

The flip side: when Whiting shut down on a transformer failure in February 2024, the WCS discount to WTI widened from $18.10 to $19.00 per barrel on CalRock brokerage marks in a single session, on fears of lost heavy-crude demand. Midwest refinery demand is the marginal bid under the barrel.

The same mechanism showed up in September 2026: with Exxon's Joliet refinery offline after a power outage, US refiners processed less crude and Canadian crude imports fell the most week on week. When Midwest runs drop, Canadian barrels are the first to feel it.
bullets.source: Tim Dallinger (EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report summary)

bullets.text: Competing heavy barrels are getting cheaper at the margin: Vitol and Trafigura, the trading houses marketing Venezuelan crude under the US-controlled export regime, were bidding Brent minus $18 to $20 a barrel for Merey cargoes bound for the US and Europe in late September, seeking steeper discounts as record tanker rates squeezed their margins. The two houses together moved about 597,000 barrels a day in August, more than half of Venezuela's roughly 1.17 million b/d of exports. A discounted Merey offer competes directly with WCS for the same Gulf Coast coker slots.

The competing barrel is a true substitute: Merey 16 runs about 16 degrees API with 2.5 to 2.7 percent sulfur, against WCS at about 21 degrees API and 3.5 percent sulfur. Merey is heavier but slightly less sour — both are delayed-coker feeds, and Merey is the grade US Gulf Coast coking refineries were built to run.
bullets.source: Oil & Gas Journal (Merey assay); FuelBridge Merey 16 datasheet, Paraguaná lab Apr 2025; Oil Sands Magazine (WCS spec)

bullets.text: The displacement is showing up in US import data: US imports of Venezuelan crude ran 583,000 to 782,000 barrels a day in the two weeks to September 18, landing directly into PADD 3. One syndicated market report put the WCS Houston discount more than $3 a barrel wider since the January announcement as refiners opted for cheaper Venezuelan barrels — treat that figure as reported, not verified; the checkable version is the ICE ARV–TMW spread.
bullets.source: EIA WPSR Table 8 (via local pipeline); marketminute syndicated report Jan 22, 2026 (secondary)

bullets.text: Russia is set to extend its ban on most diesel exports beyond the end of September as Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries continue, with an extension of a month or more under consideration, according to people familiar with the matter. The move is cross-verified: the Russian business daily Vedomosti reported on Sep 16 that the ban would run to October 31, citing delayed refinery maintenance and the need to rebuild winter fuel reserves, and Energy Intelligence reported on Sep 18 that an October extension was likely.

Imperial Oil scheduled full turnarounds at two Canadian refineries in 2026: the 197,000 barrel-per-day Strathcona refinery near Edmonton in Q2, and the 124,000 barrel-per-day Sarnia refinery in Q3 and Q4.
bullets.source: Oil and Gas Journal (citing Imperial Oil 2026 guidance)

bullets.text: Irving Oil's 320,000 barrel-per-day Saint John, New Brunswick refinery, Canada's largest, began a two-month turnaround in September 2026 running to mid-November, an extended maintenance window over its historical 30 to 35 day turnarounds.

US refinery maintenance typically peaks in October, but shipbroker Gibson reported very little confirmed for autumn 2026 because robust margins kept refiners from taking units offline. US utilization was 97.4%, the highest since 2018. The only confirmed PADD 3 turnaround was Exxon's Beaumont fluid catalytic cracker (FCC) and hydrotreaters for about 45 days from early December to mid-January.

Gulf Coast plants ran so hard in the first half of 2026 that deferred work accumulated: catalyst replacements, heat exchanger cleaning, and inspections all compressed into the September to November window. Facilities that ran the most Venezuelan heavy crude face heavier than normal coker and hydrocracker maintenance.

gaps: Forward crack spreads, such as the roughly $44 per barrel six-month forward quoted in August commentary, are trader marks, not published by the EIA. The EIA publishes historical price series, not forward margins.
Refinery-level crude slates, including how much WCS each PADD 2 plant runs, are proprietary. The market only sees the effect when a plant goes down.
Turnaround schedules are voluntary disclosures. Shipbroker Gibson notes not all maintenance is reported, so the fall calendar is always incomplete.
